title: Who is Katy Marchant? Olympic gold medallist retires at 33 ahead of LA28 Olympics to return to family farm with husband Rob
text: Katy Marchant (via Getty) Katy Marchant has announced her retirement from professional cycling at the age of 33. The Leeds-born track cyclist leaves the sport after a career filled with Olympic, World Championship and European success. Her biggest achievement came at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she won gold as part of Great Britainâs womenâs team sprint squad. Marchant also won an Olympic bronze medal in the individual sprint at Rio 2016. After 13 years at the top level, the mother of two has decided not to continue chasing a place at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. Instead, she will spend more time with her husband Rob and their children on the family farm. Who is Katy Marchant? Katy Marchant was one of Britainâs leading track cyclists for more than a decade. She represented Team GB at three Olympic Games and collected medals across some of the biggest competitions in the sport. Her first Olympic medal came at Rio 2016. Marchant won bronze in the individual sprint and established herself as one of Britainâs leading track sprinters. Eight years later, she reached another major milestone at Paris 2024. Marchant helped Great Britain win gold in the womenâs team sprint. The victory completed one of the biggest goals of her career. Her successful 2024 campaign did not end with Olympic gold. Marchant also won gold medals at the World Championships and European Championships. However, her career was also marked by a serious crash in late 2024. She later battled back to professional cycling. Marchant continued competing after becoming a mother of two. She had given birth to her second son a year before this summerâs Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. At the 2026 Commonwealth Games, she won silver in the team sprint. But the event also gave her a feeling that her professional career could be coming to an end. Marchant said, âIâve done this for 13 years, I am 33, and I have achieved more than I could have dreamt of.â She also explained that retirement had become clear to her, âWhen I thought about retirement in the past, I said to myself: âYouâll know when you know. Youâll just know.â And guys, I know.â Marchant admitted there were discussions about continuing until LA 2028. However, she did not want to make the sacrifices required for another Olympic cycle. âIâm incredibly proud of where I have got to and what I have done. I donât want to keep making those choices to do what it takes to get to LAâ, she said. title: âFeels a little crazyâ: Double Olympic winner Tatjana Smith comes out of retirement, eyes LA Olympics 2028 goal after âmissing the waterâ
text: Tatjana Smith (via Getty) Tatjana Smith has announced a surprise return to competitive swimming after initially retiring following the Paris Olympics 2024. The double Olympic champion is now targeting the 2028 Los Angeles Games, where she hopes to compete in the newly added 50m breaststroke event. Smith is South Africaâs most decorated Olympian. She won 200m breaststroke gold and 100m silver at Tokyo 2020 before adding 100m breaststroke gold and 200m silver at Paris 2024. However, her comeback is not guaranteed. Smith says LA 2028 is her goal, but she must first rebuild her race and qualify for the Games. Tatjana Smith targets new 50m breaststroke challenge Tatjana Smith initially walked away from swimming after the Paris Olympics. She had already achieved major success across two Olympic Games and was a former 200m breaststroke world record holder. However, retirement did not last as she expected. The South African swimmer said she eventually realised that she missed competing and being in the pool. That feeling helped convince her to begin another chapter in her career. The decision also comes with a completely different Olympic target. Smith is focusing on the 50m breaststroke, a new Olympic distance that gives her an opportunity to compete in an event without a long history of her own. âItâs definitely a new challenge, a new event, a new race, but also a new me,â she said. The change is significant for Smith. Her biggest Olympic achievements came in the 100m and 200m breaststroke events. At Tokyo 2020, she won the 200m breaststroke gold medal and took silver in the 100m. Three years later, she added another Olympic title in Paris. Smith won gold in the 100m breaststroke and finished with silver in the 200m. Those results made her one of the most successful swimmers in South African Olympic history. Now, she wants to create a different story in the shorter event. âFor the first time, I am choosing swimming and I am choosing the event and I am choosing a new event, that has no history but to try and write some new history. LA 2028 is the goal. It is not a promise. I still have to build a race, qualify and earn my place back on those blocksâ, she said in a video. title: 'The sport wasnât ready to let go of me': Lovlinaâs journey from Paris heartbreak to Asian Games gold
text: Asian Games Gold medallist India's Lovlina Borgohain (Image: REUTERS) NISHIO: For her 29th birthday, Lovlina Borgohain had already decided what she wanted to gift herself. Gold. On Friday, at the Nishio Gymnasium, she unboxed it herself. âItâs a special birthday for me. Iâm feeling very, very happy. I wanted to give myself a gold medal for my birthday, so I put my 100% into getting it,â she said, moments after beating Chinaâs Ziyi Bao 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg final. It was a gift that carried considerable weight given that its 265-gram medal would see Lovlinaâs maiden Asian Games title, making her only the second Indian woman after Mary Kom to fetch it. Lovlina, who had already fought several bouts in her mind, was reminded of the three inside the ring on Friday, she ticked that final box too. It was a dominant performance, but a fight in every sense. Lovlina ducked, punched, fell, picked herself up and kept coming, throwing everything at Bao before securing a unanimous 5-0 verdict. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback Not many had given the boxer from Baramukhia village in Assam a serious shot at gold. But then, Lovlina has never been much of a people pleaser. What made the victory sweeter was that it represented more than the medal, the validation of a change in mindset. After her quarterfinal exit at the Paris Olympics in 2024, Lovlina hit her lowest point. She publicly apologised for failing to win a medal, faced criticism and began to feel that her career was slipping away. Somewhere along the way, she changed the way she looked at boxing. The weight of expectations gave way to the simple joy of doing what she loved. âIt was that low which carried her all the way to gold. With the gold medal glittering around her neck, she told TOI, âFor 15 years, there were many ups and downs. I took boxing as a challenge. I had to win, then enjoy. When you work so hard and lose, you start feeling horrible that youâve given the game your everything and still havenât been able to get the medal you worked for,ââ she said. âThatâs the feeling I got after Paris. Thatâs when I thought I wouldnât be able to compete again and stayed away for months. But when I wanted to walk away from boxing, the sport wasnât ready to let go of me. title: Mary Kom  to Lovlina: Two generations, one boxing legacy
text: Lovlina Borgohain Guwahati: Lovlina Borgohain has followed a path that bears striking parallels with the legendary Mangte Chungneijang Mary Kom . But the two Indian boxing icons have built their legacies across different eras, weight categories and career trajectories. Separated by 17 years and about 350 kilometres, Mary Kom and Lovlinaâs boxing careers trace a strikingly similar arc, from modest farming households in two of Indiaâs most remote corners to international debuts that both began with silver medals. Kom, now 41, has not competed in any events and is already past IBAâs 40âyear ceiling for elite amateur boxing. Lovlina turned 29 on Friday. Kom was born in Kangathei village in Moirang in Manipur âs Bishnupur district, to Mangte Tonpa Kom, a tenant farmer. Borgohain was born in Bara Mukhia village in Assam âs Golaghat district, to Tiken Borgohain, a small-scale businessman and farmer. The parallel sharpens once their careers begin. Kom made her international debut in 2001 at the first-ever AIBA Womenâs World Boxing Championship in Scranton, Pennsylvania, at just 18 years old, in the 48kg category, winning silver in her very first appearance on the world stage. Lovlinaâs international debut came in 2013 at the Nations Womenâs Junior Cup in Serbia in the 70kg category, where she too won silver, at age 17, almost the same age as Kom, with the same colour medal, on debut. Komâs debut was immediately at the senior World Championship level, but Lovlinaâs senior international bow came five years later, in 2018, at AIBA Womenâs World Boxing Championship in New Delhi, where she won bronze in the 64kg category in her maiden senior appearance. Mary Kom was Indiaâs trailblazer on the Olympic stage, winning bronze at the London 2012 Games in the 51 kg category. Nine years later, Lovlina became only the third Indian boxer to win an Olympic medal when she claimed bronze at Tokyo 2021 in the 69kg division. Mary Komâs international dominance stretched over a much longer period. Her six World Championships gold medals remain the defining statistic of her career, alongside Olympic bronze and multiple Asian titles. Lovlina was forced into the 75kg category after the 69kg division was dropped from the Paris Olympics programme. She adapted quickly, winning Asian Championships gold in 2022 and becoming world champion at 75kg in 2023. She also won Asian Games silver in Hangzhou in 2023 to secure her Paris quota. At Paris 2024, however, Lovlinaâs campaign ended in the quarter-finals after a defeat to Chinaâs Li Qian, who eventually won the gold medal. The two careers intersect at one significant milestone, both becoming Olympic medallists and world champions, making them the only Indian women boxers to combine those achievements. For Lovlina, it is not about comparison with Mary but more about extending a legacy. Mary opened the Olympic door for Indian womenâs boxing; Lovlina became the next generation to walk through it. title: Persistence shapes Lovlinaâs the road to Asiad gold
text: Guwahati: Persistence, not speed, is what shaped a 13-year journey from an international debut to an Asiad gold. Each title arrived after an earlier attempt that fell one rung short, a pattern that defines Lovlina Borgohain âs career more than any single result. Thirteen years after her international debut, Borgohain has joined Mary Kom as the second Indian woman boxer to win an Olympic medal and gold at the World and Asian Championships and Asian Games . After Bhogeswar Baruahâs feat in 1966, she is also the second Assamese athlete in six decades to win an individual Asian Games gold. From a junior silver at the Nations Womenâs Junior Cup in Serbia in 2013 to boxingâs biggest titles, Borgohainâs rise has been defined by repeated comebacks after falling one step short. She beat Chinaâs Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg final to turn her previous Asian Games silver into a gold and end a 12-year wait for Indian womenâs boxing since Mary Komâs victory. The Asian Games title was the one major international crown missing from her collection. Borgohain had already won World and Asian Championship gold, as well as an Olympic bronze. She finished with silver at the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou. The Paris Olympics in 2024 brought another setback. Borgohainâs route to the title was repeatedly interrupted by narrow reversals. Her boxing journey began in 2012, when coach Padum Boro spotted her at a Sports Authority of India trial at her school. She began training at the Netaji Subhas Regional Centre in Guwahati that year and won gold at the Indian Womenâs Junior National Championships. In 2017, she won bronze in the 69kg category at the Asian Championships in Vietnam, marking her senior international debut. The following year, she won a World Championship bronze after exiting the Commonwealth Games in Australia in the quarter-finals. Borgohain initially took up Muay Thai, following her twin sisters, Lima and Licha. An SAI scouting programme later redirected her to boxing, recognising in the teenage kickboxer the reflexes and build the sport required. title: Lovlina turns 29 with golden punch, ends Assamâs 60-yr wait by matching Baruah feat
text: Lovlina Borgohain after winning the gold medal Guwahati: Olympic medallist Lovlina Borgohain ended Assam âs six-decade wait for an individual Asian Games gold medal on Friday, defeating Chinaâs Bao Ziyi 5-0 in the womenâs 75kg boxing final at the Aichi-Nagoya Games. The victory, secured on her 29th birthday, made Lovlina only the second Assamese athlete to win individual gold at the Asian Games after Bhogeswar Baruah, who triumphed in the 800m at the 1966 Bangkok Games. Baruahâs winning time of 1:49.4 was a Games record and earned him the distinction of becoming Assamâs first Arjuna Award recipient. Assam did win an Asian Games gold in the intervening years, with sprinter Hima Das finishing first in the mixed 4x400m relay at Jakarta 2018. Lovlinaâs triumph, however, is the stateâs first individual Asian Games gold since Baruahâs historic victory. For Lovlina, the medal completes a remarkable comeback after her quarterfinal loss in Paris olympics in 2024. Lovlina is only the second woman Indian boxer after Mary Kom to combine an Olympic medal, a World Championships title, an Asian Championships title and an Asian Games gold. She is also the first Indian woman boxer to reach back-to-back Asian Games finals, converting her 2023 silver into gold in 2026. Her father, Tiken Borgohain, said the win was especially emotional because Lovlina had wanted to change the colour of the silver she won at the previous Games. âToday also happens to be her birthday. She had spoken about winning this gold,â he said, thanking those who had prayed for her success. CM Himanta Biswa Sarma , while congratulating Lovlina, said, âThere can be no bigger gift to oneself on a birthday than bagging the ultimate honour for the country. We are so proud of you, Lovlina! The nation is proud of you and celebrates this achievement. Assam awaits your glorious return.â Assam Police on its official X handle wrote: âOur very own DSP Lovlina Borgohain strikes GOLD!..Youâve made Assam Police, Assam and the entire Nation proud!.â Lovlina was appointed as a deputy superintendent of police in Assam Police in 2022 following her medal at Tokyo Olympics. title: Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 comeback in doubt as Joscelyn Roberson tells her to âstay with your husbandâ
text: Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 comeback in doubt as Joscelyn Roberson tells her to âstay with your husbandâ Simone Biles is still undecided about competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, but a message from former US teammate Joscelyn Roberson has given her another reason to think about life away from gymnastics. Roberson reminded Biles that she does not have to return and can instead stay home with her husband, Jonathan Owens. Biles, 29, has not ruled out a fourth Olympic appearance, and she recently tested a difficult skill in the gym that made a comeback feel possible. But the decision also involves her family plans, the demands of training and what she wants from the next stage of her career. Simone Biles quotes Joscelyn Roberson on LA 2028 Olympic return Biles has competed at three Olympics, starting with Rio 2016 before Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. A return in Los Angeles would give her a chance to compete at a home Olympics and become the first American gymnast to appear at four Olympic Games. But Roberson, who was Bilesâ teammate and roommate, is not trying to convince her to return. Instead, she has been encouraging Biles to enjoy her life away from the sport. âHey babes, youâre good. Remember, you donât have to come back. Stay at your house and stay with your husband,â Biles quoted Roberson to The Associated Press. Biles has admitted that she is still trying to work out what she wants. In September, she told The Associated Press, âI feel like itâs kind of in the works which way Iâm leaning towards.â Her decision is also tied to her life with Owens and her plans to start a family. Biles said those personal matters have to be considered alongside the physical demands of preparing for another Olympics. âI am getting to the age of 30 where we start to talk about, âWhat does your reproduction cycle â¦ whatâs going on in there? What does that look like? How healthy is it?ââ she said. âAnd so I think these are major things that are on the table at my age that I have to take into consideration and weigh those options and what that looks like and when we want to start a family.â Simone Biles says recent gym attempt made decision harder There is also a part of Biles that still wants to know what she can do. She recently went into the gym with her sister Adria and attempted a double layout. She landed it and said she was surprised by how little fear she felt. And of course I was like, what the h**l? That wasnât that bad. Like, I wasnât as scared as I thought I was going to be. And that scared me more with the decision.â Biles also knows that a return could affect younger gymnasts competing for places on the 2028 US Olympic team. âI know some of the girls would be like, âOh no, Simoneâs coming back,ââ Biles said. title: Gujarat awards Rs 1.3 crore to Elavenil Valarivan for dual silver success in Japan
text: Elavenil Valarivan poses with her silver medal after arriving at Terminal 3 of Indira Gandhi International Airport in New Delhi on Friday, September 25 Gandhinagar: Rifle shooter from Gujarat, Elavenil Valarivan , was felicitated with a cash award of Rs 1.3 crore by deputy chief minister Harsh Sanghavi on Monday for her two-silver-medal-winning performance at the 2026 Asian Games that is currently being held in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, Japan. Valarivan won silver medals in the womenâs 10m air rifle individual and team events. Quoting Sanghavi, an official statement said the Gujarat govt was committed to providing its sporting talent with the training and facilities required to compete at the global level. He also credited the parents for playing a crucial role in supporting their childrenâs sporting journeys. Sanghavi noted that Valarivan had studied at Sanskardham, a complex functioning under the govtâs district-level sports school (DLSS) scheme, and said her achievements would inspire thousands of young sportspersons in the state. The 25-year-old shooter, who lives in Ahmedabadâs Maninagar area, has been associated with Gujaratâs Shaktidoot scheme since 2017-18 and currently figures in its âAâ category. The state govt said she has received Rs 1.3 crore under the Shaktidoot and Olympic promotion schemes and another Rs 74 lakh through DLSS and Khel Mahakumbh schemes, taking the total assistance to Rs 2.4 crore. Valarivan represented India at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympics. She won gold at the 2019 ISSF World Cup in Rio de Janeiro with a score of 251.7. The athleteâs achievements also include medals at the Junior World Cups in Suhl, Germany, in June this year and Sydney, Australia, in 2018. She also won medals at the Asian Airgun Championship at Shymkent in Kazakhstan, World University Games in Chengdu and competitions in Munich in 2025. She was also conferred the prestigious Arjuna Award in 2022. title: "I would bleed": Simone Biles breaks down over painful skin battle that left her âmiserableâ before the Olympics
text: Simone Biles (Getty Images) Simone Biles has opened up about a deeply personal health struggle that continued for years while she trained and competed at the highest level. The Olympic champion revealed that persistent itching and flaking eventually became so severe that she would scratch until her skin bled. What she initially believed was dandruff later led to diagnoses of seborrheic dermatitis and eczema. Now, Biles is using her experience to encourage people dealing with similar symptoms to stop dismissing them and seek professional dermatological care. Simone Biles reveals how her skin condition affected her Biles said her symptoms began several years ago while she was preparing for the 2024 Paris Olympics. She first noticed itching and flaking around her scalp and assumed dandruff was the cause. Instead of immediately seeing a dermatologist, Biles tried several over-the-counter products. They did not provide the relief she hoped for, and the problem eventually spread beyond her scalp. âI was itching and flaking. I would itch so hard and use a comb that I would bleed. I was just like, âI canât live like this. Iâm itching. Iâm miserable. I feel uncomfortable. I need to see someone who can give me relief,â â Biles tells PEOPLE ahead of the campaign launch on Tuesday, Sept. 29. The symptoms became especially difficult during her Olympic journey. With millions watching her compete, Biles worried that the visible flaking would be noticed on television. âI didnât go to the dermatologist immediately because Iâm so busy,â she says. âI was always in the gym, I was always traveling, so I didnât take that step, but it finally got so bad. At the Olympics, I was flaking everywhere, so I was afraid that someone would see it on the TV... thatâs why I finally went.â Biles was eventually diagnosed with seborrheic dermatitis affecting her face and scalp, along with eczema on her arms. She now manages the conditions with prescribed treatments. Simone Biles wants others to seek professional help Biles is sharing her experience through the Skin to Believe In campaign, launched in partnership with Arcutis Biotherapeutics. Her goal is to help people recognise that persistent skin symptoms may need more than home remedies. Dr. Angela J. Lamb, a board-certified dermatologist who joined Biles for the discussion, said delayed diagnosis can make these conditions harder to manage. She also noted that severe scratching can create additional risks. âI think Simoneâs story really mirrors what I see with patients,â Dr. Lamb says. âThe delay in diagnosis only makes things worse. Simone should not have been having her scalp bleeding. Luckily she didnât get any infections from that, but sometimes that can lead to infection.â Lamb also addressed a common misunderstanding surrounding these conditions. Seborrheic dermatitis and eczema are not contagious, meaning they cannot simply be passed from one person to another through everyday contact. âItâs not an infection. Itâs not contagious,â says Dr. Lamb. âSo sharing combs with folks or a bed or a pillow, itâs not like youâre going to transfer it... and same for eczema or atopic dermatitis, itâs not an infection.â For Biles, opening up about the experience is about making it easier for others to ask for help. âOnce we know that we canât fix every problem on our own, itâs okay to get help,â she tells PEOPLE. âOnce we raise awareness, then they can get that relief that they deserve. Thatâs really what itâs about, not silently suffering. There is help out there for you.â Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines She has one simple message for anyone struggling with ongoing symptoms. âWe just have to take that first initiative to go see a dermatologist and to get that relief because they deserve that,â she says. âThese are the trusted professionals... theyâve worked their whole entire lives to treat people for these causes. Itâs just incredible that we have these resources.â âOnce you do, itâs so easy,â Biles adds, insisting, âYou just have to make the appointment.â Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news , check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule . title: A 42-year-old record, a truckerâs daughter: Vithya Ramraj breaks PT Ushaâs mark and rewrites history

The 27-year-old Indian hurdler clocked a personal best of 54.75 seconds to win bronze in the women's 400m hurdles at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, breaking the national record that had belonged to legendary Usha since August 1984. In 2023, at the Hangzhou Asian Games, Ramraj had clocked 55.42 seconds to claim bronze and equal Usha's mark set at the Los Angeles Olympics on August 8, 1984. That record had stood for 39 years at the time. Watch Vithya Ramraj targets Asian Games gold, eyes 53-54 seconds in 400m hurdles Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | Schedule Now, in Nagoya, Ramraj went one better, shaving 0.67 seconds off the old national record en route to her second individual Asian Games 2026 medal. The medal also adds to Ramraj's Asian Games record. She had won bronze in the women's 400m hurdles at the 2023 Hangzhou Games to go with to silver medals in the 4x400 relay and mixed events. A truckerâs daughter who refused to give up Vithya grew up in a modest family, with her father working as a truck driver. Her mother enrolled Vithya and her twin sister Nithya, a 110m hurdler, at the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu hostel in Erode. Athletics was not a carefully planned choice. âAt a parent-teacher meeting, my PE teacher suggested sports for us. My mother chose athletics since it offered more visibility than team games. title: New beginnings, new heroes: Women lead India's charge as a new generation shines in Nagoya
text: Lovlina Borgohain and Neeru Dhanda (Image credit: X) As Neeru Dhanda led the Indian contingent out for one last time at the Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on Sunday night, it was symbolic of how Indiaâs Asian Games campaign had unfolded over the past two weeks. The women had come to the fore - packing punches, vaulting to new heights, lifting weights, taking aim, towering over opponents with sixes, blazing the track, finding the fairway and hitting the back of the net. Indiaâs final tally of 85 medals, including 21 gold, may represent a drop from the 106 medals and 28 golds won in Hangzhou. But numbers alone cannot tell the story of these Games. Watch Lovlina Borgohainâs golden birthday: Asian Games medal after comeback There were path-breakers everywhere, athletes who pushed through glass ceilings that had stood for years. The aftermath will bring reviews, reflections, deliberations and reports. But before the analysis begins, it is only fair to celebrate those who made these Games count. For almost 12 days, the Indian gold rush had remained subdued. Then, just as the sun finally began showing up in Nagoya, the floodgates opened. Eleven gold medals came in the final two days, transforming what had threatened to become a disappointing campaign into a collection of stories about guts, resilience and glory. Dhanda, the 26-year-old from Sangatpura in Haryana, had set the tone by winning Indiaâs first individual gold of these Games in the womenâs trap event. The women went on to win 11 gold medals, apart from the three secured in mixed events. The contingent had 83 debutants, who accounted for 41 of Indiaâs 85 medals â a clear indication of a changing guard across several sports. But if one athlete were to be picked as the face of that change, it would be difficult to look beyond 17-year-old Kumkum Mohod. The Maharashtra archer won two gold medals and a silver, but her biggest achievement went beyond the medal tally. She ended South Koreaâs two-decade domination of the womenâs recurve events by becoming the first Indian to win individual recurve gold at the Asian Games. It did not take her long to make the biggest stage of her young career her own. Even her Korean opponent Oh Ye-jin, whom Kumkum beat for the individual gold, was left impressed. âFor a 17-year-old, she is very composed and has a very bright future,â Oh said. Another teenager, Prithika Pradeep, also emerged with two gold medals, adding to the sense that a new generation is beginning to announce itself. Pranavi Urs became the first Indian woman to win an Asian Games golf gold. Behind every medal was a story of humble beginnings, survival in sport, societal pressures overcome and personal tragedies endured. That made the successes more than just entries in a medal table. The comeback girls They were not newcomers to the big stage. They had competed at the biggest of them all â the Olympics. But Nagoya offered unfinished business. Lovlina Borgohain had contemplated walking away from boxing after a difficult phase post the 2024 Paris Olympics. Instead, she returned to punch her way to gold. Parveen Hooda, returning after a doping ban, produced her own golden comeback. The bronze she had won in Hangzhou and subsequently lost became gold in Nagoya. Mirabai Chanu did not win gold, but her silver in the 49kg category had the weight of a championâs achievement. It also completed her Asian Games medal collection. Golden standards The womenâs kabaddi team survived a tense battle against Iran. The womenâs hockey team ended a 44-year wait for Asian Games gold. And Harmanpreet Kaur and her team ensured that cricketâs gold returned to India. Yet, for all the celebration, there were glaring blanks. Manu Bhaker, one of Indiaâs biggest sporting heroes, returned without a medal. There were plenty of nearmisses and some disastrous outings. Indiaâs badminton return of a solitary bronze was another disappointment, particularly with a strong menâs doubles combination of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, PV Sindhu and Lakshya Sen in the squad. title: Two gold at 13: Yu Zidiâs rise and Summer McIntosh rivalry dominate swimming talk, but youngest Asian Games record remains unclear
text: Yu Zidi (Reuters/AP Photo) At just 13, Yu Zidi is already swimming towards a rivalry that could define the next era of women's swimming. The Chinese teenager claimed her second gold medal at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games on Monday, winning the women's 200m individual medley in 2:06.10 â a time that took her to within 0.40 seconds of the world record held by Canadian Olympic champion Summer McIntosh. The result has only intensified the anticipation around a potential Yu-McIntosh showdown. The two could meet as early as next year's World Aquatics Championships in Budapest, before the spotlight turns to the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where Yu would still be only 15. McIntosh, who won three individual gold medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024, owns the world records in all three events Yu is targeting: 2:01.65 in the 200m butterfly, 2:05.70 in the 200m individual medley and 4:23.65 in the 400m individual medley. Watch TOISA Spotlight | Miraj Ahmed Khan on Olympic gold, setbacks, Rio 2016 and the fight that continues Yu closes in on McIntoshâs world record Yu's latest gold came less than 24 hours after she won the 200m butterfly in a Games-record 2:05.08. She will also compete in the 400m individual medley later this week. Her rapid rise has already taken her onto the biggest international stage. At the 2025 World Championships in Singapore, Yu competed at just 12 and finished fourth in all three individual events she entered. She also became the youngest-ever World Championships medallist by winning bronze as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team. Earlier this year, she added another eye-catching result by defeating American Regan Smith in the 200m butterfly at a meet in China. Smith had won silver in the event at the Paris Olympics. The comparisons with McIntosh are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore. Hong Kong's four-time Olympic medallist Siobhan Haughey said the emergence of swimmers like Yu reflects an exciting trend in the sport, pointing to McIntosh's own rise as a teenager. "When Summer first started she was also very young and swimming fast, so I think that's kind of the trend these days," Haughey said. Youngest Asiad gold medallist? Records don't have the answer Yu's achievements have naturally raised another question: is she the youngest athlete ever to win an Asian Games gold medal? For now, there is no definitive answer. Asian Games officials said records dating back to the inaugural edition in New Delhi in 1951 are incomplete, making it impossible to establish whether Yu is the youngest gold medallist in the history of the continental Games. She is not even the youngest competitor at Aichi-Nagoya. That distinction is believed to belong to 11-year-old Japanese esports competitor Yuki Kurihara. So while Yu is making history in the pool, the broader age record remains unresolved. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Chinaâs swimming machine keeps producing stars Yu's emergence also underlines China's extraordinary depth in Asian swimming. China won a record 28 swimming gold medals at the Hangzhou Asian Games in 2023, finishing well ahead of South Korea's six and Japan's five. The Chinese dominance has continued in Aichi-Nagoya, with the country winning five of the seven swimming golds on Monday after taking six of seven on Sunday. But Yu's story is bigger than China's medal tally. At an age when most swimmers are still developing towards senior international competition, she is already challenging the world's fastest and being discussed in the same breath as McIntosh. For now, McIntosh remains ahead on the stopwatch. But with Yu only 13, the gap is already shrinking â and the swimming world may be watching the beginning of a rivalry that could stretch all the way to Los Angeles. title: Bigger than the Paris Olympics: Asian Games 2026 kicks off with 11,000 athletes, 43 sports and some very different games
text: Glimpses from Asian Games 2026 opening ceremony. (Reuters Photos) The Asian Games are officially underway in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Saturday and the numbers alone tell part of the story: this is a sporting event that is bigger than the Paris Olympics in athlete participation, while also offering a programme that looks markedly different from the world's biggest multi-sport spectacle. More than 11,000 athletes are expected to compete at the 20th Asian Games, compared with about 10,700 at the 2024 Paris Olympics. That does not make the Asian Games bigger than the Olympics in prestige or global reach. But by the sheer number of athletes taking part, the continental showpiece has once again crossed the Olympic mark. And the scale becomes even clearer when the programme is considered. Watch Asian Games: Sehdev Yadav reveals how SAI arranged rooms for Indian athletes A total of 43 sports featured at Aichi-Nagoya, with athletes from 45 countries and regions competing from September 19 to October 4. The Games also include an OCA Refugee Team. The official opening ceremony took place on Saturday, but competition had already been underway for more than a week in some disciplines. Basketball began on September 10, while football also started well before the ceremony, underlining one of the biggest differences between the Asian Games and the Olympics: the enormous programme forces several competitions to begin before the formal curtain-raiser. ALSO READ: How Indiaâs Asian Games medal story has changed over two decades 11,000+ athletes: Bigger than Paris, but not quite Hangzhou The most striking number in Aichi-Nagoya is the athlete count. The Paris Olympics featured about 10,700 athletes. The Asian Games have more than 11,000, making the continental event larger in terms of athlete participation. Organisers have not released a final official athlete total, but they have indicated that more than 11,000 athletes are registered. The number could ultimately approach the scale of the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, China, where roughly 12,000 athletes competed in 2023. That puts Aichi-Nagoya in an unusual position. It is larger than the Olympics by athlete participation, yet it is also a very different event in terms of geography, sporting culture and the range of disciplines on offer. The Games involve 45 countries and regions, stretching from Afghanistan to Yemen, along with the OCA Refugee Team. Japan has the largest delegation, with 933 athletes. China is sending 815 athletes. Hong Kong, despite having a population of about 7.5 million, has around 580 athletes. China arrives as the dominant force from the previous edition. At Hangzhou, it won 201 gold medals, followed by Japan with 52 and South Korea with 42. India was next with 28 gold medals, while Uzbekistan won 22 and Taiwan 19. Members of India's contingent walk during the opening ceremony. (AP Photo) 43 sports: Olympic favourites meet Asian specialities The sheer number of sports is another reason the Asian Games can feel unlike the Olympics. There are plenty of familiar Olympic disciplines. Athletics, swimming and football remain central parts of the programme, alongside other established sports. But then there are sports that give the Asian Games a distinctly regional identity. Kabaddi , for instance, is a major Asian team sport combining speed, strength and physical contact. Sepaktakraw blends elements of volleyball and football, while kurash, an ancient form of wrestling originating in Uzbekistan, adds another traditional discipline to the programme. ALSO READ: Five little-known sports India will compete in at Asian Games 2026 The organisers have also made room for newer and less familiar events. Teqball, a sport that combines elements of table tennis and football, is making its Asian Games debut. Virtual taekwondo, padel and mixed martial arts are also part of the programme. Esports returns after making its debut at the Hangzhou Asian Games. That combination is one of the defining features of the continental event. The programme can move from athletics and swimming â sports at the heart of the Olympics â to kabaddi, sepaktakraw, kurash and teqball, all within the same Games. It is also one reason the schedule has become so demanding. Basketball began on September 10, more than a week before Saturday's opening ceremony. The men's basketball semifinals were played on Friday, a day before the Games were officially declared open. Football has also been underway for several days. The first gold medal of the Games is expected on Sunday, with the triathlon among the events likely to produce the first champion. Swimming will also provide one of the early highlights, with China's 100m freestyle world-record holder Pan Zhanle and 13-year-old sensation Yu Zidi among the names attracting attention. Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which serves as a floating temporary athletes' village. (Reuters Photo) A very different athletes' village The scale of the Asian Games is not limited to the competition programme. A total of 17,000 athletes and officials are being accommodated across Japan. But unlike the Olympics, Aichi-Nagoya does not have a traditional dedicated athletes' village. Instead, accommodation has been spread across hotels, converted wooden containers and a cruise ship. The Costa Serena, an Italian cruise ship, is functioning as a floating athletes' village and can accommodate up to 5,000 athletes and officials. The arrangement is part of a broader effort to contain costs after the Tokyo Olympics, for which Japan officially spent $13 billion. A government audit suggested the actual figure could have been twice that amount. But the unusual accommodation arrangements have also become one of the biggest talking points before the Games. Athletes and officials have complained about cramped rooms, small beds and logistical problems. Some delegations have reported leaks in the converted wooden accommodation, while others have raised concerns about transportation and long journeys to training venues. South Korea said the containers at Garden Pier were too cramped for its basketball players. Delegations have also complained about registration delays, late buses and athletes being sent to incorrect venues. India's cricket authorities arranged separate hotel accommodation for the men's team because of the tight allocation of beds. The problems have added to the scrutiny surrounding the build-up, although the Olympic Council of Asia has described them as teething difficulties. Asian Games Teqball (AP Photo) A 16-day sporting festival with a distinctly Asian identity The Asian Games will run until October 4, bringing together more than 11,000 athletes across 43 sports and 45 participating countries and regions. Nagoya, Japan's third-largest metropolitan area after Tokyo and Osaka, is hosting the event. The metropolitan area has a population of about 9.5 million and is located roughly 350 kilometres south of Tokyo. The opening ceremony at Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium provided the official starting point after a buildup marked by organisational problems. Emperor Naruhito formally declared the Games open, with Empress Masako, IOC president Kirsty Coventry and OCA president Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani among the dignitaries present. Japan's father-and-son hammer-throwing duo Shigenobu Murofushi and Koji Murofushi jointly lit the cauldron at the conclusion of the torch relay. But the real measure of the Games will come over the next 16 days. The Asian Games may not carry the same global prestige as the Olympics, but Aichi-Nagoya demonstrates why they remain a sporting giant in their own right. title: Simone Biles questions Olympic gymnastics tie-break rules after Paris 2024 result as LA 2028 decision nears
text: Simone Biles questions Olympic gymnastics tie-break rules after Paris 2024 result as LA 2028 decision nears Simone Biles wants one simple change in Olympic gymnastics before the 2028 Los Angeles Games: if two athletes finish with the same score, both should receive the medal. Biles made the point after remembering her balance beam result at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she and Suni Lee both scored 13.100 but were ranked fifth and sixth. With Biles still unsure about returning in 2028, the rule remains one part of gymnastics she would like to see changed. Simone Biles wants ties to mean shared Olympic medals During an interview with HELLO! on September 11, Biles was asked whether there was a gymnastics rule she would change. Her answer was direct: âIf itâs a tie, both people get the medal.â The comment connects to what happened in the balance beam final in Paris. Biles and Lee both finished with 13.100 points, but Biles was placed fifth because her execution score was higher. Biles had a 7.200 execution score, while Lee had 6.900. Both had the same difficulty score of 6.200. Under the rules used at Paris 2024, a tie in an apparatus final was first decided by the higher execution score. If that was also equal, the difficulty score was used. If the gymnasts were still level, they shared the same classification. The International Gymnastics Federation (FIG) listed those steps in its Paris 2024 rules. The system has changed over the years. Tied gymnasts once could receive the same medal, but the International Olympic Committee (IOC) introduced tie-break procedures for judged sports after the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, with gymnastics adopting a new system in 1997. One of the clearest examples came at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. Nastia Liukin and He Kexin both scored 16.725 on uneven bars, but He won gold after a detailed tie-break process based on judging deductions. The Washington Post later described the system as an âobscure tiebreaker.â Simone Bilesâ LA 2028 decision remains uncertain Bilesâ comments come while her own Olympic future is still open. The 29-year-old has not confirmed that she will compete at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. In September, she returned to the World Champions Centre in Houston and posted videos of herself doing flips while joking that she was checking whether she âstill got it.â At Paris 2024, Biles won four medals: three golds and one silver. She also finished fifth on beam after a fall. If she does return for LA 2028, she would be 31, but her decision will involve more than age or physical ability. title: The peaks are higher, the floor is rising: How Indiaâs Asian Games medal story has changed over two decades
text: India at the Asian Games (AI generated representative image) âAbki baar, sau paarâ was the rallying cry when India arrived at the Hangzhou Asian Games in September 2023. By the time the Games ended, it had become more than a slogan. India had crossed the 100-medal barrier for the first time in its Asian Games history, eventually finishing with 106 medals â 28 gold, 38 silver and 41 bronze. The 100th medal came through the women's kabaddi team, which defeated Chinese Taipei in the gold-medal match. It was India's biggest-ever medal haul at the Asian Games. Watch Asian Games 2026: Triple jumper Praveen Chithravel shifts focus after CWG silver medal But as India prepares for Aichi-Nagoya 2026, the more important story is not that India finally reached 100. It is that 100 no longer looks like an isolated miracle when viewed against Indian sport's larger trajectory. Hangzhou came after four consecutive editions in which India had already crossed 50 medals. India is becoming increasingly consistent. At the Asian Games, 50-plus medals have become the norm. At the Olympics, India has produced multiple medals at five consecutive editions for the first time. India remains an under-achiever. But the direction of travel is increasingly difficult to ignore. From occasional highs to a new Asian Games floor The strongest evidence of India's sporting evolution is perhaps the simplest: 53 > 65 > 57 > 70 > 106. Those are India's medal tallies at the last five completed Asian Games â Doha 2006, Guangzhou 2010, Incheon 2014, Jakarta 2018 and Hangzhou 2022. Before this run, India had crossed the 50-medal mark only twice in the previous 14 editions. Both came at home. At the inaugural Asian Games in New Delhi in 1951, India won 51 medals, including 15 gold. When New Delhi hosted the Games again in 1982, India collected 57 medals, including 13 gold. It took another 24 years for India to cross 50 again. Doha 2006 changed that. India won 53 medals in Qatar, finally breaking the half-century barrier away from home. It was followed by 65 in Guangzhou, 57 in Incheon and 70 in Jakarta and Palembang. Then came Hangzhou. The five consecutive 50-plus medal campaigns represent something India had never previously achieved at the continental event. That is arguably more significant than the 106 itself. A record medal tally can be an extraordinary peak. Five consecutive campaigns above a particular benchmark point towards a structural change. India has therefore entered Aichi-Nagoya with a different kind of expectation. Another 106 may be difficult, particularly with a 499-athlete contingent compared with the 661 who travelled to Hangzhou. But the benchmark has moved. The question is no longer simply whether India can cross 50. It is whether a 50-medal campaign would now be considered underwhelming. Hangzhou did not just breach 100 â it moved India's ceiling The jump from Jakarta to Hangzhou was extraordinary. India went from 70 medals in 2018 to 106 in Hangzhou, an increase of 36 medals. But the gold-medal jump arguably tells an even more significant story. India won 16 gold medals in Jakarta. In Hangzhou, it won 28. That is a 75 per cent increase in gold medals in one edition. And India's Hangzhou medal haul (106) was twice its Doha tally (53) over a 17-year period. The 100-medal barrier, therefore, should not be viewed in isolation. India's Asian Games ceiling has moved. It would be unrealistic to treat 106 as an automatic target every time India enters an Asian Games. But if India can produce another 70-plus campaign in Aichi-Nagoya, it would create another significant benchmark â three consecutive editions above 70. That could eventually make 70-plus the next version of what 50-plus has become today. One ceiling becomes the next floor. The medal base is becoming broader There is another part of the Asian Games story that is easy to miss when the conversation is dominated by the overall tally. India is not merely winning more medals. Its medal-producing ecosystem is gradually becoming broader. Historically, athletics has been India's biggest Asian Games sport by a considerable distance, with 283 medals. Shooting follows with 80, wrestling with 65, boxing with 61 and lawn tennis with 34. Athletics remains the giant. But recent editions have shown that India's medal ambitions are increasingly supported by multiple disciplines. Hangzhou was an excellent example. Athletics produced 29 medals, shooting contributed 22 and archery added nine. More importantly, shooting produced seven gold medals, one more than athletics' six. That shows the modern Indian medal base is not entirely dependent on its biggest traditional discipline. Wrestling, boxing, squash, archery and tennis have repeatedly provided medal opportunities, while athletics and shooting continue to contribute. The Commonwealth Games in Glasgow in 2026 provided another encouraging indicator for boxing, with Indian boxers winning 10 medals, including seven gold â their best-ever gold-medal haul at the event. India's sporting rise is becoming less dependent on one discipline or one generation. That is what a broader sporting ecosystem looks like. The Olympics tell a quieter story of progress If the Asian Games provide the dramatic version of India's sporting evolution, the Olympics provide the subtler one. India has won only 41 medals across its entire Olympic history â 10 gold, 10 silver and 21 bronze. For a country of India's size and sporting ambitions, that remains underwhelming. But look at when those medals have arrived. From Beijing 2008 through Paris 2024, India won 24 of its 41 Olympic medals â 58.5 per cent of its entire Olympic medal haul in just five editions. Beijing 2008 produced three medals. London 2012 delivered six. Rio 2016 dropped to two. Tokyo 2020 produced a record seven. Paris 2024 ended with six. The numbers are not spectacular by the standards of sporting superpowers. But historically, they are significant. Before this five-edition run, India had achieved multiple-medal campaigns at only two Olympics â Paris 1900, when Norman Pritchard won two silver medals, and Helsinki 1952, when India won one gold and one bronze. Then came five consecutive Olympic editions with multiple Indian medals. That is the quieter revolution. And the country is no longer disappearing between Games. The consistency itself represents progress. Paris showed how close India remains to a bigger breakthrough The six-medal haul at Paris 2024 was disappointing because expectations had changed. After India's record-breaking Asian Games campaign a year earlier, there was genuine hope that the country could finally push into double figures at the Olympics. It did not happen. But Paris also showed why the ambition for 10 medals was not completely misplaced. India had several agonising near-misses. The archery mixed team finished fourth after losing its bronze-medal match. Lakshya Sen lost the badminton bronze-medal match. Shooter Arjun Babuta finished fourth in the men's 10m air rifle. Manu Bhaker, already a double medallist, missed out on a third medal after finishing fourth in the women's 25m pistol. India's skeet team lost its bronze-medal shoot-out, while weightlifter Mirabai Chanu finished fourth. Then came Vinesh Phogat's disqualification before her gold-medal bout after she was found 100 grams over the weight limit. Seven âwhat ifâ moments. That does not mean India should retrospectively count those as medals. But it demonstrates how narrow the margins can be at the Olympics. Four of those near-misses becoming medals would have taken India to 10. The more important takeaway is that India is beginning to produce enough finalists and medal contenders across different sports for the conversation to shift from âCan India win?â to âHow many can India convert?â That is a different challenge. And in many ways, it is a sign of progress. The real evolution: India's floor is rising The Asian Games and Olympics operate on completely different scales, but together they reveal a striking change in India's sporting story. The underlying pattern is comparable. India's old sporting story was one of sporadic success. Its emerging story is one of sustained presence. At the Asian Games, India has established a 50-medal floor. Hangzhou then pushed the ceiling beyond 100. At the Olympics, India has established something much more modest but historically important: five consecutive Games with multiple medals. That is why the central story of India's sporting evolution should not simply be âIndia is winning more medals.â It is that India is becoming increasingly consistent at winning medals. India is not there yet. The Olympic record remains underwhelming. But the direction is unmistakable. The floor is rising. Aichi-Nagoya is the next test India will enter Aichi-Nagoya 2026 carrying the weight of its greatest Asian Games campaign, but the objective should not simply be to reproduce Hangzhou's 106. A 499-athlete contingent is heading to Japan, compared with 661 in Hangzhou. That difference makes a direct comparison difficult. The more meaningful test is whether India can sustain the performance level that has emerged over the last two decades. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Can 50-plus remain the floor? Can 70-plus become the new expectation? Can more sports join the traditional medal pillars? Those are the questions that matter beyond the medal table. India may still be an under-achiever. But it is increasingly difficult to argue that the country is standing still. The medals are still not enough. The Olympic haul is still too modest. The Asian Games success still needs to be sustained. The conversion rate at the highest level still needs improvement. But the pattern has changed. From occasional Asian Games peaks to five consecutive 50-plus campaigns. From two historic multi-medal Olympics to five in a row. From a narrow collection of medal sports to a gradually expanding base. The peaks are getting higher. More importantly, the floor beneath them is rising. Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. title: Who are Simone Bilesâ parents? The story of Ronald and Nellie and their bond with the gymnast
text: Who are Simone Bilesâ parents? The story of Ronald and Nellie and their bond with the gymnast Simone Bilesâ success in gymnastics has been tied to the support of her parents, Ronald and Nellie Biles. The couple adopted Simone and her younger sister, Adria, when Simone was six after she spent years in foster care. Ronald and Nellie gave her a stable home and encouraged her gymnastics talent from the beginning. They also became a constant presence at her competitions and supported her during difficult moments, including her Tokyo Olympics withdrawal. Years later, they remained by her side as she returned to competition and won medals at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Ronald and Nellie Biles adopted Simone when she was six Ronald and Nellie met in 1977 while Ronald was serving in the Air Force in San Antonio, Texas. Nellie was studying nursing at the time. Ronald was already a father to Simoneâs biological mother, Shannon. The couple married on Jan. 16, 1977, and later had two sons, Ronald Jr. and Adam. Simoneâs early childhood was difficult. Her biological mother struggled with drug and alcohol addiction and could not care for her four children. Simone and her siblings were placed in foster care. Simone spent three years in the foster care system and later spoke about being hungry and afraid during that period. Ronald and Nellie eventually adopted Simone and her sister Adria and moved them to Houston, Texas. Simone has said that this change gave her a second chance at life. She also made clear how important her adoptive parents became to her. Nellie once described the emotional change that happened after the adoption. She said that telling children you love and care for them is only words at first. For her, motherhood became real when she realized she would do anything for the children. Simone later said that her parents âsaved meâ and thanked them for supporting her from the beginning. She also described them as role models who showed her what a strong foundation of love and support looks like. Ronald and Nellie supported Simoneâs gymnastics career Simone first tried gymnastics when she was six after visiting a gym during a daycare field trip. Coaches noticed her ability and sent home a note encouraging her to take classes. Ronald and Nellie quickly signed her up. Nellie later recalled that Simone rarely wanted to miss practice. Even when Nellie suggested that she stay home because she was sick, Simone would insist on going. Simone also said her parents made sure she had what she needed to compete at her best. Ronald and Nellie became regular faces in the stands. Simone said her parents had never missed one of her competitions until the Tokyo Olympics, when COVID-19 restrictions prevented them from traveling to watch her. Their absence made the Tokyo experience harder for Simone. She withdrew from several events after experiencing the âtwistiesâ and focused on her mental and physical health. She later said that not having her parents there was one of the things that made the experience especially difficult. Nellie said 17 family members traveled to support Simone. Ronald also became a lighthearted part of the Olympic coverage when he was seen using binoculars from the stands. Simone later called the moment âsoooo freaking cute.â Ronald and Nellie have also played a role beyond simply cheering from the stands. title: '15 years ... I waited for long': Krishna Jayasankar set for her India moment at Asian Games
text: Krishna Jaisankar (Image credit: Agencies) Whenever Krishna Jayasankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt. It has one word written on it: INDIA. Every time she looks at it, her eyes get moist. But there is also a sense of confidence that builds within her. After waiting for 15 years, Krishna knows that when she finally wears the India jersey in Japan, it will mean much more than simply making her Asian Games debut. Watch 'I'm walking in as a medal contender, not a participant': Krishna Jaisankar on her Asian Games debut For the 23-year-old shot putter, the jersey will represent 15 years of ups and downs, missed opportunities, injuries and countless moments when she had to pick herself up and start again. âIt's a surreal feeling. I just can't wait to don that jersey in Japan. 15 years.... I waited for long and yes, I have earned it. I am very appreciative, like I'm very grateful for the opportunity and to be able to finally put Team India on my back,â Krishna told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview. After missing out on selection several times, Krishna finally broke through and earned her place in the Indian team for the Asian Games 2026. Now, as she prepares to travel to Japan, the Indian shot putter wants to leave the old disappointments behind and write a new chapter - one that she hopes will end with a medal. Her message to herself when she reaches Japan is simple. âAll right, it's showtime,â Krishna said. A long road to the India jersey Krishna's journey has never been an easy one. There were moments when she wanted to give up. She left India at a young age, first moving to Jamaica and later to the United States, as she looked for opportunities to develop as an athlete. Then came the Commonwealth Games opportunity. Krishna was among the favourites to make it to the big event, but a hamstring injury disrupted her plans. She tore her hamstring just three weeks before the event. Yet, she returned to competition and managed to qualify for the Asian Games. She also became the national champion after 15 years. âI just think the fighter mentality that I have. Never to give up. Never to settle. Setbacks are meant for something. Setbacks are supposed to mould you, but not define you,â she said. Paris 2024 became a turning point The biggest setback came in 2024. Marred by injuries, Krishna missed the Paris Olympics. But the difficult phase also forced her to look closely at herself and rethink the way she was approaching her career. She began paying more attention to her nutrition, sleep and recovery. She also started spending more time reflecting and talking to herself. âIt was a very rough period for me,â she said. âI left my country, left my family, left my comfort zone. What does my opportunity cost? What am I getting back? I'm not making the team, I'm not competing. Why am I getting injured?â she said. That period eventually changed her approach towards her ultimate goal - representing India. Instead of looking too far ahead, Krishna decided to take things one step at a time. âIf you've got a dream, you've got to protect it. You have a dream, you've got to protect it,â Krishna said. From a basketball family to shot put Krishna grew up in a sporting family. Her parents, Prasanna and Jay Shankar, have been involved in basketball, and she closely watched the work they put into developing the sport. Her mother has also been a national selector for Indian basketball. But Krishna eventually chose athletics and found her own identity in shot put. âI think my inspiration was within my corners, which is my family. Whatever I am today it is because of their support. I wanted to choose a different sport and I did and I am really happy about it,â she said. âThanks to the Reliance Foundation, the Athletics Federation of India, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu, and everyone in Tamil Nadu. Everybody has supported me and believed in me,â the 23-year-old said. Chasing Asian Games glory Making her Team India debut at the Asian Games is a special moment for Krishna. But she does not want the excitement of finally making the team to overshadow her bigger target - winning a medal. Once she is in Japan, she wants to treat the competition like any other championship. âNow it's go time, there is no look back. I am looking forward, looking ahead in the future,â she said. âIt's going to be a show, man. It's going to be a show from all sectors of athletics. Let it be track, let it be field, we're going to put up a show. All we ask in return, support us. Keep us in your prayers,â Krishan said. Olympics - the ultimate dream For Krishna, the Asian Games is not the end goal. It is a start. Her bigger dream is the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. She carries an Olympic chain with her even though she is yet to compete at the Games. For her, it is a reminder of where she wants to go. âI'm not an Olympian, but every single day I aspire to be one. I'm confident now I can say that that dream is no longer a dream. It's like, I'm converting it to be a reality,â she said. The chase for 18 metres Krishna won a gold medal at the National Federation Cup 2026 and, in the process, broke her own record of 17.09m. She won the top prize with a personal best throw of 17.35m. Now, Krishna has set herself the target of crossing 18 metres. She believes the Asian Games 2026 will be a great platform to achieve that feat while also challenging for the gold medal. âI am getting closer,â she said. âBut again, it's very important to believe in the process. No better place to do it than Japan. Let's have a PB in Japan. I know I am a medal contender,â she said. âSo, the mindset also is walking into the thing and be like, you know what, I'm walking in as a medal contender, not as a participant,â she said. Bodyshaming: Turning comments into strength Krishna has been muscular since childhood. Her appearance sometimes made her uncomfortable. She felt that she did not fit what she believed was society's traditional idea of how a woman should look. âI didn't even know the meaning of body shaming until, you know, somebody came and told me, hey, somebody's body shaming you,â she said. But over the years, Krishna learned to see her body differently. The same body that some people made fun of became the body that helped her break records and earn her place in Team India. âTo show the world, to show the society, that the body that you're making fun of and making me feel that I'm ashamed of is the body that's helping me break records, is the body that's helping me debut for Team India at the Asian Games,â she said. Her message to young girls is direct. She also has another message: do not live for other people's approval. Do not seek validation from people because again, comparison is a thief of joy,â she said. title: Tajinderpal Singh Toor misses third straight Asian Games gold, dedicates silver to 10-month-old daughter
text: Image credit: Instagram Tajinderpal Singh Toor came close to a third straight Asian Games gold in the menâs shot put but settled for silver in Nagoya. The 31-year-old threw 20.64 metres, finishing behind Iranâs Mohammadreza Tayebise, who took gold with 20.81 metres and broke Toorâs previous Games record. For the Indian champion, the medal carried a deeper meaning. He dedicated it to his 10-month-old daughter, calling her the lucky charm who changed his familyâs story after two difficult losses. A medal dedicated to his daughter Toor spoke about the personal weight behind the silver. âThis medal is for my daughter Rabab Kaur Toor. My wife lost two babies during her pregnancy, in 2022 and in 2024. Rabab has been the lucky mascot for me,â he told The Indian Express from Nagoya. 22 Sept 2026 | 14:56 Does your child tell you everything about school? What helps them open up? Rabab was born last November. Her arrival brought joy after the pain of two miscarriages that had left the coupleâs dream of becoming parents shattered. Holding the Tricolour and folding his hands in prayer once the final positions were confirmed, Toor made clear that the medal belonged to the little girl who had become his source of strength. A bittersweet day on the field Toorâs best throw of 20.64 metres was solid, yet it was not enough to defend the title he had won in Jakarta in 2018 and again in Hangzhou. In 2018 he set a Games record of 20.75 metres. That mark was bettered on Saturday by the Iranian athleteâs 20.81-metre effort. When it became clear he would finish second, Toor responded with quiet dignity. He posed for photographs with the national flag and acknowledged the result. The day was bittersweet, but it still placed him on the podium for a third consecutive Asian Games . Answering doubts after a difficult season Earlier this year Toor had finished only third at the Inter-State National Championships in Bhubaneswar, behind Karamveer Singh and Samardeep Gill. Questions about his form had begun to surface. âPeople had started talking after my performance at the Inter-State. This medal is an answer to all those who questioned my ability. Winning a third Asian Games medal is a special feeling,â said Toor, who hails from Khosa Pando village in Moga district. Karamveer, the other Indian in the final, placed tenth. On the biggest stage of the season, Toor delivered when it counted. Competing through a career of injuries Injuries have followed Toor throughout his career. Before the Commonwealth Games he suffered a Grade-One calf tear. An MRI confirmed the damage after the event. âPrior to CWG, I suffered a calf strain, and post the CWG, the MRI revealed that it was a Grade-One tear. I manage by adjusting technique. My coach MS Dhillon tells me never to stop,â he explained. The list is longer. A groin injury before the Tokyo Olympics, pain when he set the Asian Games record, a calf muscle tear at the Asian Championships in Bangkok, a knee problem before Hangzhou, and an ankle injury six months before Paris. âMy career and injuries go together,â he said. This year he has crossed 20 metres nine times and recorded one throw beyond 21 metres. His personal best remains 21.77 metres from 2023. He still believes more is possible. âI know I have a 22m throw in me.â For an athlete who has repeatedly returned from setbacks, the silver in Nagoya felt like another hard-earned step forward and one he was glad to share with his daughter. title: Medals bring relief in Valarivan household
text: Saroja Valarivan (left), mother of Elavenil Valarivan, celebrates her win, in Ahmedabad on Sunday. Ahmedabad: A sense of palpable relief enveloped the Valarivan household in southern Ahmedabadâs Khokhra locality after ace shooter Elavenil Valarivan clinched silver medals in Aichi-Nagoya. Elavenil had returned empty-handed from the three major multi-sporting events, the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta, 2020 Tokyo Olympics and the 2024 Paris Olympics, which she had participated in. Elavenilâs mother Saroja told TOI, âBecause of the last two shots, she missed the gold. A medal at the Asian Games was missing. In the 2018 edition in Jakarta, her rifle malfunctioned and she missed out the 2022 edition (held in 2023 because of Covid) in Hangzhou. This is the one medal she and we wanted her to win badly. We are relieved.â Despite the double podium finish, there was no big celebration in the Valarivan household. âHer father is happy and excited that she has finally won an Asian Games medal. There werenât huge celebrations on Sunday also. All family members watched the shooting event at their respective homes. We will plan a gathering after Elavenil comes back on Sept 26 after the conclusion of the 10m air rifle mixed team event,â said Saroja. Her medals mirror the achievement of Gagan Narang, whose Gun for Glory academy she trains at. Narang had won two silver medals in corresponding events in the menâs category at the 2010 Asian Games in Guangzhou. Asked about the significance of the 27-year-oldâs achievement, Narang told TOI, âFantastic. Iâm quite happy because I know what she has gone through to get to this particular medal. We believed in her, kept our head down, put in the work and let the performance do the talking. âEla chose to put her blinders on to shut out the distractions and worked really hard.â And, the result was there to see at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery. She used to train for four hours a day at the academy. She would spend another hour or two working on her physical strength,â Rohit Havaldar said. Sonam now joins Kolhapurâs rich shooting tradition. title: 'Haar nahi maanunga': Sujeet Kalkal's Asian Games 2026 gold mission on the road to LA Olympics
text: For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Haryanaâs Bhiwani district. NEW DELHI: The last time Sujeet Kalkal came close to an Olympic dream, he never even got the chance to step on the mat. Now, as he prepares for his maiden Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the 23-year-old wrestler is looking at the continental event as the first major marker of a new Olympic journey - one that he hopes will eventually take him to Los Angeles in 2028. âAsaan nahi tha, bhaisaab. Fir se start kiya hai, haar nahi maanunga. Olympics to sapna hai, poora karna hai bass [It wasnât easy. Iâve started again, and I wonât give up. The Olympics is a dream, and I have to fulfil it, thatâs all],â Sujeet told TimesofIndia.com ahead of the Asian Games. There is reason for that confidence. Sujeet enters Aichi-Nagoya having established himself among the leading wrestlers in the 65kg category. He won the Asian Championships in Bishkek earlier this year and has continued to build his credentials in 2026. He also won the 65kg selection trials for the Senior World Championships in Lucknow last week, beating Anuj Kumar 8-3 in the final. The Asian Games, however, will present a different test. Sujeet's 65kg category features some of the biggest names in Asian wrestling, including Japan's Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka. Sujeet's competition starts from October 2, when the men's freestyle 65kg, 86kg and 125kg categories will be contested. For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Imlota village in Haryanaâs Bhiwani district. âI was very happy to qualify [for the Asian Games] . It is a fresh start, and I will not disappoint. Behind this success is the hard work of my father, my coach and my entire team. I am in good form. I will come back with the gold medal,â Sujeet said. âThe 65kg category is a very challenging and competitive weight category. The worldâs best wrestlers always compete in this category. But I have complete faith in my hard work and preparation. My entire focus is only on gold, brother. I have worked very hard,â he added. It will also be a chance to measure how far he has travelled since April 2024, when a three-day ordeal at Dubai International Airport ended his first Olympic campaign before it had even begun. Three days at Dubai Airport It was April 2024. Sujeet was at Dubai International Airport, waiting to continue his journey to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he was scheduled to compete in the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. But record rainfall had caused floods in Dubai and badly disrupted air travel. Sujeet was stranded at the airport. He could see water everywhere and could only pray that the situation would improve so he could travel to Bishkek, where the qualifiers were scheduled to take place. Sujeet could only watch the time, calculate the days and hours on his fingers, and then sit back. His connecting flight was delayed and eventually remained stranded at the airport for three days. A flight was finally arranged, but by the time he reached Kyrgyzstan and then the venue, it was one and a half hours after the weigh-in had been completed. The Wrestling Federation of India and officials tried their best to find a way to get Sujeet into the competition. But the United World Wrestling rules left them with no option. The opportunity was gone. âI felt very bad. I have no words. It was four years of hard work, and it all ended in that one moment. I was in good form, and everything was over in a moment. I cried alone too, but I had faith in God. I explained things to myself and returned to India,â Sujeet said. Father's words gave him strength Sujeet returned to India devastated. At home, his father Dayanand was waiting for him. Dayanand, a former Greco-Roman wrestler, knew what his son was going through. Sujeet immediately hugged his father. He became emotional and had his father's shoulder to cry on. His father hugged him and told him: âKoi nahi beta, fir se mehnat karenge hum, Olympics khelna haiâ. Those words stayed with Sujeet. âI didn't give up' Starting again was not easy, but Sujeet was adamant. He won gold at the United World Wrestling Ranking Series in Budapest in the menâs 65kg division at the start of 2025. He added two more gold medals to his tally in Zagreb and at the Tirana Grand Prix. He then won a gold medal at the World U23 Championships in 2025 in Novi Sad, Serbia, followed by another gold at the Asian U23 Championships in Vung Tau, Vietnam. He didn't stop there. Sujeet became Asian Champion after winning gold in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. With that gold medal finish, he also rose to the No. 1 ranking in the world. Now, he is set for his first Asian Games. A medal in Aichi-Nagoya would take him another step closer to his next big target - the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. âI didn't give up. I have worked very hard. I have to go a long way. If I had competed in Paris, I would have been 21. I am 23 now. I will be 25 when the Los Angeles Olympics comes around. Age makes a big difference. But I don't want to step back. My mindset is still the same â to win a medal for the country,â he said. Sujeet was just five when he was pushed into the 'akhaada'. Dayanand could not go to the Olympics to represent India. Now, he wants his son to fulfil that unfulfilled dream. âPapa is very strict," he says. "Wo dangal mein haanikarak baapu they na, wo waise hi kuch hain (laughs). He told me, âSon, you have to become a wrestler. A wrestlerâs son should be a wrestler.â I have learnt a lot from him since childhood. He is both my guru and my father. Whatever I am today is because of him,â he said. âHis dream is to see me at the Olympics and see me win a medal. I will definitely fulfil this dream of my father,â Sujeet signed off.
