title: âWe should not waste our energyâ: Manu Bhaker urges Indian athletes to look beyond Asian Games chaos
text: Manu Bhaker (AFP Photo) NEW DELHI: Shooting ace Manu Bhaker has urged her fellow Indian athletes to put the organisational issues surrounding the Asian Games behind them and focus on competition, saying the continental showpiece represents a âonce in a lifetime opportunity and experienceâ. The build-up to the Games in Japan has been marred by complaints from athletes and officials of several participating countries, including India, over cramped accommodation, organisational mismanagement and long travel times between hotels and training venues. Watch Asian Games: Sehdev Yadav reveals how SAI arranged rooms for Indian athletes With criticism mounting over the arrangements, Bhaker called on the Indian contingent not to allow the problems to distract them from their performances. âTo all my fellow athletes from India, we will have some issues. I saw a couple of issues circulated in social media and people telling me these are the issues,â Bhaker said in a video message posted by the Indian Olympic Association. âRegardless of whatever the issues we have, this is probably a once in a lifetime opportunity and experience. We have to make sure that we enjoy the time rather than complaining,â she added. âWe should not waste our energyâ Bhaker, a double Olympic medallist, said Indian athletes had worked too hard to reach the Asian Games to allow the organisational difficulties to consume their attention. âWe have prepared the best we can and so we must try to perform the best we can. We have worked so hard to be here and we should not waste our energy in pointing out that this is not right and that is not right. Medal may come or not, that is another story, but we must give our best.â The 24-year-old has been given another significant responsibility at the Games after being named one of India's two flag bearers for Saturday's opening ceremony. Bhaker created history at the Paris Olympics in 2024 when she became the first athlete from Independent India to win two medals at a single edition of the Olympic Games. She won bronze in the women's individual 10m air pistol and mixed team 10m air pistol events. Manu Bhaker to lead India's contingent as flag bearer The Asian Games will also carry a strong personal significance for Bhaker, who is competing at the continental event for the third time. âWhen I came to know of this (being chosen as one of the flagbearers), I had flashbacks of my earlier days. When I started, I never thought I would reach this far one day. It's definitely feeling proud and honoured,â she said. âI was just 16 years old when I competed in the Asian Games in 2018. This is my third Asian Games. I was in Palembang (Indonesia) in 2018 and so could not attend the ceremony.â Bhaker recalled that her late coach Jaspal Rana had allowed her to attend opening ceremonies of multi-sport events only when she was a flag bearer, given the tight competition schedule for shooters. title: How Stephen Curry built his $350 million fortune? His $62.6M salary, $400M Li-Ning deal and lavish investments
text: Stephen Curry. Image via: Ezra Shaw /Getty Images Steph Curry has turned a remarkable NBA career into a vast business empire. The Golden State Warriors star is now estimated to have a net worth of $350 million , while his 2026-27 NBA salary stands at $62.6 million . His wealth extends far beyond basketball, with major endorsement deals, media ventures, investments and his own brand adding to his income. After more than a decade at the top of the sport, Curry has also secured another major contract that could take his career NBA earnings close to $650 million by 2029. Stephen Curry net worth and NBA salary Stephen Curry's current financial position reflects how much his value has grown since entering the NBA in 2009. The Warriors selected him seventh overall in the draft, and his first professional contract was modest compared with the deals he would later command. His breakthrough extension came in 2012, when Golden State gave him a four-year contract worth about $44 million. At the time, Curry was still dealing with concerns about recurring ankle problems. The contract soon became one of the most valuable bargains in NBA history. Curry developed into an MVP, won championships and changed the way teams approached three-point shooting while playing under that deal. His earning power changed dramatically in 2017. Curry signed a five-year, $201.2 million contract, becoming the first NBA player to agree to a deal worth more than $200 million. Four years later, he went even further. His four-year, $215 million extension made him the first player in league history to sign two contracts worth more than $200 million. Curry's latest extension arrived in September 2026. The two-year agreement is worth $116 million and begins with the 2027-28 season. It includes a player option for 2028-29. Based on those contracts, Curry's career NBA salary could reach approximately $648.7 million through the 2028-29 season if he exercises the option. Stephen Curry's $400 million Li-Ning deal NBA salary is only one part of Stephen Curry's financial story. His endorsement portfolio has become just as important to his overall wealth. Curry started his professional career with Nike before moving to Under Armour in 2013. His rise to superstardom helped turn that relationship into a much larger business opportunity, eventually leading to Curry Brand. That partnership later changed. Curry Brand became independent after the relationship between Curry and Under Armour ended in 2025, although Under Armour continued selling previously developed products during 2026. Curry then landed another huge deal. In June 2026, he signed a 10-year endorsement agreement with Li-Ning worth more than $400 million . The partnership covers more than basketball shoes. It includes apparel, lifestyle products, golf and plans to expand Curry Brand retail operations in China and the United States. The agreement is worth more than $40 million per year on average, giving Curry another major source of income outside his Warriors contract. Celebrity Net Worth estimates that Curry also earns around $30 million annually from endorsements , although the exact amount can vary from year to year. His commercial portfolio includes partnerships with companies such as Fanatics, Google, JPMorgan Chase, Panini, Rakuten and 2K Sports. Stephen Curry's business empire beyond basketball Curry has also built businesses that give him influence away from the court. His wider ventures operate under Thirty Ink, covering areas such as media, branding, investments and philanthropy. One of his best-known projects is Unanimous Media, which Curry founded with Erick Peyton in 2018. The company works across film, television, documentaries, publishing and podcasts. Its projects often focus on sports, family and faith. Curry has also explored entertainment in front of the camera. He played a fictionalised version of himself in the Peacock comedy "Mr. Throwback" and released the book "Shot Ready" in 2025. His business interests also include Gentleman's Cut bourbon and Underrated, a platform designed to give overlooked young athletes greater access to competition and development opportunities. That business approach has helped Curry build an identity that reaches well beyond his basketball statistics. His career has become a combination of sport, entertainment, branding and investment. Stephen Curry's career, championships and real estate Stephen Curry's wealth would not be possible without the basketball career that created his global profile. He has won four NBA championships , two regular-season MVP awards and the 2022 NBA Finals MVP. He was also the first unanimous MVP in NBA history after his historic 2015-16 campaign. That season remains one of the most memorable individual years in modern NBA history. Curry averaged 30.1 points per game, made 402 three-pointers and helped Golden State win 73 regular-season games. In 2021, he passed Ray Allen to become the NBA's career leader in made three-pointers. He later reached another historic milestone by becoming the first player to make 4,000 regular-season three-pointers in March 2025. Curry added an Olympic gold medal to his rÃ©sumÃ© at the 2024 Paris Games, helping Team USA win the men's basketball tournament. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines His success has also shaped his property portfolio. Curry and his wife, Ayesha, have completed several major real estate transactions in California. Among their notable purchases was a $31 million Atherton estate bought in 2019. They later sold another Atherton property for $29.1 million in May 2026 after purchasing it for $30 million in 2020. The couple have also owned homes in Oakland, Orinda, Walnut Creek, Alamo and Menlo Park, along with a luxury condominium in San Francisco. Away from business and basketball, Curry and Ayesha have focused heavily on philanthropy. They founded the Eat. Learn. Play. Foundation, which supports children through programmes involving food, education and physical activity. Curry's financial rise therefore tells a larger story than a list of contracts. His NBA salary created the foundation, but endorsements, entrepreneurship, media and investments have helped turn one of basketball's greatest shooting careers into a much broader financial empire. title: Who is Fariba Hashimi? Meet the Afghan cyclist who trained disguised as a man and won Asian Games silver after fleeing Taliban
text: Who is Fariba Hashimi? Meet the Afghan cyclist who trained disguised as a man wins Asian Games silver after fleeing Taliban. For Fariba Hashimi, becoming a top cyclist didnât start with dreams of gold medals or crossing epic finish lines; it started with figuring out how to ride a bike at all. Growing up in northern Afghanistan, just riding meant risking her safety. She and her sister, Yulduz, wanted to train, but for girls that meant disguises: baggy clothes, faces hidden behind layers of masks. Even then, just one trip down the road could easily end with people hurling insults, or worse: actual stones. The threats were constant. But Fariba wasnât easily discouraged. The sisters kept showing up, dodging harassment and occasional violent attacks. Once, a rickshaw driver drove straight at them. Sometimes, they used fake names just to enter small competitions because even their family didnât approve at first. Still, winning those secret races caught the attention of the Afghanistan Cycling Federation. Eventually, their father drove them to Kabul so they could try out for the national team. Then, everything changed. When the Taliban returned in 2021, life for ambitious women shrank overnight. Afghan girls and women lost school, lost work, lost access to public life itself. Eventually, Fariba and Yulduz had to flee their home, with help from Alessandra Cappellotto, an Italian world champion cyclist. Settling in Italy gave them safety, but their roots and dreams always pointed back toward Afghanistan. On September 22, 2026, standing on the podium in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, Fariba wasnât just another cyclist with a medal. After years of hiding, sheâd earned silver in the Asian Games womenâs road race: the first Afghan woman to claim any Asian Games medal since 2002. It meant something far beyond winning a race. Fariba beat out dozens of competitors, coming in just behind Chinaâs Guo Li, with Hong Kongâs Leung Wing Yee in third. But for her, the result was personal, as well as political. She explained why so simply after the race: âThis silver medal can show a lot of resilience from Afghan women,â she said, as quoted by The Guardian. âI hope the next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear.â Her words echoed the journey of so many women who have had to hide their passions and identities in plain sight, hoping someday things might be different. Who is Fariba Hashimi? Fariba started cycling as a teenager in Faryab province, inspired by her older sister. Training meant long rides with the fear of being caught, but the sisters stuck together. They shared every harsh lesson the streets had to offer. Fariba once described to journalists how sheâd stack on two or three masks to keep people from recognizing her, just for a morning ride. In their earliest races, the girls used fake names because their family feared for their safety and reputation. But as their talent grew harder to ignore, things shifted. It wasnât just about their own determination. The feats they managed, like winning first and second in local races, caught the eye of sports officials. Eventually, their family got behind them, and that tiny bit of support made a huge difference. Today Fariba lives and trains in Italy, turning her early defiance into a professional cycling career. At the Asian Games, she powered through to second place, unaccompanied by any mechanic or professional support team. She had to fix and clean her bike herself, and even leaned on the kindness of Japanese competitors for a hand with maintenance. âI was the mechanic for myself. I was washing the bike myself. Thank you to the Japanese team. They were really, really nice to me, fixed my bike,â she said. Her gratitude was obvious. Anyone whoâs been forced to go it alone understands what it means to finally have someone in your corner, even if just for a day. From hiding her identity to the Olympics Cycling took Fariba beyond any limits set for Afghan women. Not only did she escape the immediate dangers back home, but she also made the leap to international competition, representing Afghanistan all the way to the Paris 2024 Olympics. There, the Hashimi sisters joined a handful of athletes embodying two realities at once: The risk of simply being a woman with dreams in Afghanistan, and the pride of carrying that flag before the world. Even at the Asian Games, Faribaâs victory didnât come easy. She lacked a proper support team and had to rely on herself for every practical detail and setback, making her silver medal as much an achievement in grit as athletic talent. She finished seventh in the womenâs individual time trial two days before her silver: an exhausting turnaround for any athlete, but she thrived on it. Why does her medal matter? Right now, Afghanistan is the only country on Earth where girls and women arenât allowed to attend secondary school or university. They canât work in most jobs, and sport is out of the question. Since 2021, opportunities for women have collapsed; UN Women and UNESCO both say the rollbacks are unmatched worldwide. All the while, Hashimiâs success stands as something stubborn and luminous: undeniable proof that Afghan women are made for more than what the Taliban decrees. The same government that forbids women from entering a gym now watches one carry the Afghan flag across an international finish line, visible and proud. âMillions of women, from many countries, have the same dream and they are standing with me,â Fariba said. That sense of shared hope, woven through her quiet determination, speaks louder than the medal around her neck. Whatâs next for Fariba Hashimi? Anyone thinking Fariba will stop at silver is missing the point. She and Yulduz are already eyeing the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Their journeyâs never been about just one finish line; itâs about showing Afghan women everywhere that the world is bigger than their cages. She hasnât forgotten the help sheâs had, or those she leaves behind. âThe next generation will come here and represent their country without any fear,â she says, back turned to the old world, eyes locked on the future. On that podium in Japan, Fariba held more than a medal; she held a message. For every girl whoâs forced to train in secret, whoâs told she isnât allowed to be strong, her ride is a signal: Keep going. The bicycle that once was hidden now carries the dreams of an entire nation, one that refuses to be invisible. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: Asian Games 2026: India's full schedule on September 19, Saturday; Quimcy Dsouza in Teqball semifinal before opening ceremony
text: Quimcy Dsouza. (Photo/Agencies) The Asian Games 2026 will officially begin on Saturday, with the opening ceremony scheduled to start at 2:30pm IST in Nagoya. However, a few competitions, including women's cricket, soft tennis and teqball, have already got underway ahead of the ceremony. India's schedule for Saturday (September 19): Teqball 6:30am IST: Women's singles semifinal â Quimcy Dsouza vs Sumaya (Indonesia) Opening Ceremony 2:30pm IST onwards: Asian Games 2026 opening ceremony Quimcy Dsouza reaches Teqball semis; mixed doubles pair eyes bronze India's Quimcy Joaquim Dsouza moved within one win of creating history after reaching the women's singles semifinals in teqball at the Asian Games in Nagoya on Friday. Making her Asian Games debut, Quimcy upset top seed Yuina Sakamoto of Japan 2-1 (10-12, 12-11, 13-11) in her first Group A match. She followed that up with a 2-0 (12-9, 12-7) win over Cambodia's Koemyean DY in her second group match, finishing on top of Group A and booking a place in the semifinals. By topping the group, Quimcy received a bye in the quarterfinals. The 24-year-old will face Indonesia's Sumaya in Saturday's semifinal. A win will guarantee India its first-ever medal in Teqball, one of the six sports making its Asian Games debut. Even if she loses in the semifinals, Quimcy will still have a chance to win bronze on Sunday. In the mixed doubles event, Quimcy and Mohammed Anas Imran Beg were beaten 0-2 (7-12, 10-12) by Vietnam's Hoang Minh Tan Nguyen and Gia Nghi Trinh in the quarterfinals. However, the Indian pair remain in contention for a bronze medal after winning their repechage match. Teqball is one of six sports making its Asian Games debut in Aichi-Nagoya, alongside Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), Padel, Surfing, BMX Freestyle and Virtual Taekwondo. The sport combines elements of football and table tennis. It was invented in Hungary in 2014 by Gabor Borsanyi, Gyorgy Gattyan and Viktor Huszar, while the first official Teqball World Championships were held in Budapest in 2017. In Teqball, players use every part of the body except their hands and arms to rally a standard size-five football across a curved table divided by a transparent plexiglass net. title: Champions return, 314 debutants arrive: Inside Indiaâs 500-plus Asian Games campaign
text: India eye record medals at Asian Games 2026 NEW DELHI: Hoping to build on the historic campaign three years back at Hangzhou, India begins its campaign at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya with a 500-plus athlete contingent, aiming to better the 106-medal tally racked up at the last Games. While the build-up to the Games has been marred by mismanagement, an accommodation crisis and the threat of a typhoon looming large over the Japanese prefecture, for the athletes, once the Games begin, it will be, as the adage goes, âgame mode onâ. The 500-plus athlete Indian contingent comprises a sizeable group of returning champions and experienced campaigners. 314 of those athletes are preparing for their first appearance at the continental event. Watch Animesh Kujur targets Asian Games medal after breakthrough season Interestingly, women athletes make up 46.7% of the contingent. At 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the youngest member. Equestrian rider Shruti Vora, 55, is the oldest. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi will be the youngest to play for India at Asian Games (TOI Graphics) India will compete in 256 events across 36 of the 43 sports at Aichi-Nagoya, with the Games beginning on September 19 and running until October 4. Avinash Sable, returning from a year-long injury, will try to defend his men's 3000m steeplechase title, while Tajinderpal Singh Toor returns in the men's shot put. Parul Chaudhary will be another athlete trying to defend her women's 5000m crown, while India's men's 4x400m relay team will also go into the Games as defending champions. In badminton, Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty will aim to defend their men's doubles title. Their gold in Hangzhou was India's first Asian Games title in the event. Indian compound archers swept all five gold medals in the discipline at Hangzhou, and returning champion Jyothi Surekha Vennam will be the fulcrum around whom India's archery campaign will revolve. Then there are athletes whose Asian Games story is still waiting for a first chapter. India's record-breaking numbers in the last Asian Games (TOI Graphics) Mirabai Chanu âs missing Asian Games medal Mirabai Chanu has won a world title, Olympic silver and Commonwealth Games gold. title: American star Gabby Thomas apologizes on X after fan backlash for failing to recognize Usain Boltâs baby photo in Olympics quiz
text: Gabby Thomas (Image Via Getty) American sprint star Gabby Thomas has apologized after a viral Olympics social media video showed her failing to recognize a childhood photo of Usain Bolt. The Paris 2024 triple Olympic gold medalist laughed after struggling to identify the Jamaican sprint legend, leading to criticism from fans online. Thomas later addressed the backlash on X. She admitted that she was embarrassed by the moment and apologized for both not recognizing Bolt and laughing during the quiz. She also explained that she grew up watching Bolt and other Black track athletes who inspired her generation. Gabby Thomas opens up on Usain Boltâs baby photo mistake The incident happened during a promotional trivia segment shared by the Olympicsâ social media channels. Athletes were shown childhood photographs of famous track and field stars and asked to identify them. When Gabby Thomas was shown a baby picture of Usain Bolt, she could not recognize him. Her reaction included laughter, which quickly became a talking point among fans on social media. Some viewers criticized Thomas for failing to identify one of the biggest names in athletics history. Bolt is widely regarded as one of the greatest sprinters ever. He holds the world records in both the 100m and 200m and won multiple Olympic gold medals during his legendary career. As the clip continued to circulate, Thomas decided to respond to the criticism. She took to X and directly addressed the reaction to the video. âI want to genuinely apologize to everyone I upset for not recognizing Usain Bolt in his baby photo the other day on the Olympics social media video. I shouldnât have laughed about it either. I am so embarrassed. I promise to unpack this and will do betterâ, she wrote. Thomas then offered more context about her connection to Bolt and the influence he had on her generation of athletes. âI grew up watching Usain Bolt among many other Black track athletes. They inspired me and showed my generation of athletes what Black excellence looks like (on and off the track). I know what he and Noah look like- their baby photos just stumped me. But they shouldnât have. I would choose to be black in every lifetimeâ, she continued in her second tweet. title: Pak to play Asian Champions Trophy in Punjab, face India on Nov 1: CM Mann
text: Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann with Hockey Indiaâs secretary general Bhola Nath Singh, director general Cdr RK Srivastava, executive board member RP Singh and Hockey Punjab president Nitin Kohli in Mohali on Monday Mohali : Punjab will host the Menâs Asian Champions Trophy for the first time from Oct 27 to Nov 5, featuring a high-stakes clash between India and Pakistan in Jalandhar on Nov 1, chief minister Bhagwant Mann announced on Monday. Mann, who unveiled the tournament logo in Mohali alongside Hockey India officials, said the Centre permits Pakistan to compete in multi-lateral sporting events on Indian soil, even though bilateral series remain suspended The six-nation tournament features India, Pakistan, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia and China, with Oman and Bangladesh named as reserve teams. All league-stage matches will be played at Jalandharâs Olympian Surjit Singh Hockey Stadium. The action will then move to Mohaliâs Olympian Balbir Singh (Senior) International Hockey Stadium for the semi-finals on Nov 4 and the final on Nov 5. Mann said the participation of Pakistan adds immense sporting weight to the championship. âThe India-Pakistan clash at 7 pm on Nov 1 in Jalandhar will be one of the biggest attractions of the tournament,â Mann said. âAn India-Pakistan match is not about hatredâit is about the passion for hockey, the roar of the spectators, and the beauty of the sport,â he said. Hockey India secretary general Bhola Nath Singh highlighted the strong relationship between the two hockey federations. âIf the Indian team defeats Pakistan, I make it a point to meet their team first,â he shared. To support the event, CM Mann announced an allocation of Rs 25.40 crore, including Rs 22.96 crore for upgrading the venues in Jalandhar (Rs 14 crore) and Mohali (Rs 8.96 crore). He also announced free entry for all spectators to boost crowd engagement Calling the event an âemotional homecomingâ for a sport deeply rooted in Punjabâs history, Mann highlighted the stateâs rich athletic legacy. Punjab has produced more than 50 Olympic medallists and 10 national captains, including legends like Olympian Balbir Singh Sr, Udham Singh and Ajit Pal Singh, who have inspired generations, he said. âEven today, this tradition continues. During the Paris 2024 Olympics, Punjab had 10 players representing India, with Harmanpreet Singh leading the national side,â Mann added. Defending champions India enter the tournament aiming to retain their title, having previously won back-to-back championships in Chennai (2023) and Hulunbuir, China (2024). PUNJAB TO BID FOR 2030 HOCKEY WORLD CUP MATCHES: MANN Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann said India will host the Hockey World Cup in 2030 and Punjab will stake its claim to host matches of that prestigious tournament as well. âSuccessful organisation of the Asian Champions Trophy will strengthen that case. Our govt is preparing not just two stadiums, but a message for the sporting world. We have the infrastructure, the talent and sporting culture to host the big international events,â he said. title: Inspiring story of the day: "My middle school said I should be playing with dolls": How Sabrina Ionescu turned rejection into an NCAA record and WNBA championship
text: How Sabrina Ionescu turned rejection into an NCAA record and WNBA championship(Getty Images) Some inspiring sports stories begin with championships and records, while others begin with a young athlete being told there is no place for her. For Sabrina Ionescu, one of those moments came in middle school when she wanted to play basketball but her school did not have enough girls to form a team. Instead of walking away from the sport, Ionescu found another way to keep playing. Years later, she became an NCAA record-holder, the No. 1 overall pick in the WNBA Draft, an Olympic gold medalist and a champion with the New York Liberty. How Sabrina Ionescu responded when her middle school told her to play with dolls Basketball was already a major part of Sabrina Ionescu's childhood. She grew up playing with boys and also competed on a club team. Her twin brother Eddy played basketball too, and Ionescu sometimes filled in for his all-male team when they needed another player. Her middle school presented a different problem. There were not enough girls to form a team, and when Ionescu wanted to play with the boys, the school did not allow her to join them. Years later, she remembered exactly what she was told. âMy middle school said I should be playing with dolls. Seriously, word-for-word,âIonescu said in a 2019 interview with The Washington Post. The comment could have pushed a young athlete away from the sport. Ionescu responded differently. She started looking for girls who could join the team so there would be enough players for a girls' basketball team. âSo I went out and recruited a bunch of girls to sign up for the team, and then I would just play,â she said. The story was not simply about getting onto a school team. It also showed how Ionescu learned to create opportunities when they were not immediately available. Playing against boys also forced her to find different ways to contribute. She recalled situations where the boys did not want to pass the ball to her, so she focused on rebounding and creating her own chances. When she played with older athletes, she could use passing to influence the game even when she was physically smaller. Those skills later became central to her identity as a player. Sabrina Ionescu was not simply a scorer. She could rebound, pass and create plays for teammates, which eventually made her one of the most complete guards in college basketball. The girl who had once been told there was no place for her on the boys' team was already learning how to make herself useful on the court without waiting for someone else to give her an opportunity. How Sabrina Ionescu turned those early setbacks into an NCAA record Sabrina Ionescu's move to the University of Oregon took her basketball career to another level. She quickly became one of the biggest stars in college basketball and built a record that still defines her legacy. She finished her Oregon career with 26 triple-doubles, an NCAA record across men's and women's basketball. She also became the only NCAA player to reach 2,000 points, 1,000 assists and 1,000 rebounds. Her final college numbers showed just how unusual her all-around game was. Ionescu recorded 2,562 points, 1,040 rebounds and 1,091 assists during her Oregon career. The numbers were especially notable because they reflected the same skills she had developed when she was younger. Rebounding had once been a way to stay involved when teammates did not pass to her. Passing later became one of the strongest parts of her game. At Oregon, those skills helped her become a player capable of controlling a game in several ways. Her rise also brought her into the orbit of some of basketball's biggest names. Kobe Bryant became an important influence during her development, and Ionescu later spoke about how much she learned from watching his approach to the game. âHe had such attention to detail, just all the small fundamental things,â Ionescu said in an interview with Vanity Fair. Bryant's death in January 2020 came shortly before Ionescu entered the WNBA. She had looked up to him for years and later explained how much his example influenced her. That same year, another major chapter began. The New York Liberty selected Ionescu with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2020 WNBA Draft. The selection placed huge expectations on a player who had already become one of the most decorated athletes in college basketball. Her first professional season, however, did not go according to plan. Ionescu injured her left ankle in her third WNBA game and missed the rest of the 2020 season. Instead of getting a full rookie campaign, she had to spend much of the year recovering and preparing for another chance. She eventually returned to the court and continued developing into one of the Liberty's leading players. The following years brought more milestones. Ionescu earned her place among the league's top players and represented the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where she won a gold medal. But another major opportunity was waiting in New York. How Sabrina Ionescu helped the New York Liberty win their first WNBA championship The Liberty reached the 2024 WNBA Finals and faced the Minnesota Lynx in a series that went all the way to Game 5.The deciding game took place at Barclays Center, giving New York a chance to win the first championship in franchise history in front of its home crowd. The game went to overtime before the Liberty won 67-62. Ionescu's individual numbers in the deciding game were unusual for her. She shot 1-for-19 from the field and 1-for-10 from three-point range, finishing with five points. Yet she still contributed seven rebounds and eight assists while playing 39 minutes and 39 seconds. The Liberty did not need Ionescu to have her best shooting night to finish the job. New York found contributions from across the roster and secured the championship that had eluded the franchise since its first WNBA season in 1997. For Sabrina Ionescu, the championship added another major achievement to a career that had already included an NCAA record, the No. 1 overall draft selection and Olympic gold. Her story also extends beyond what happened on the court. Ionescu has spoken about wanting to give young athletes opportunities that she did not always have growing up. Through her SI20 Foundation, she has worked on initiatives connected to youth sports and education. In her Vanity Fair interview, she explained why she wanted to start that work early rather than wait until later in life. "I didn't want to wait to do it when I was 35; I wanted to start this while I was young,â she said. That idea connects with the story of her childhood. When her middle school did not give her an obvious route onto the court, she recruited girls and created another route herself. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Years later, she had the platform to help create opportunities for other young athletes. She did not respond by leaving basketball behind. She kept playing, developed an all-around game, broke NCAA records, became the No. 1 overall WNBA pick, won Olympic gold and helped the New York Liberty win their first championship. Her journey was not built around one dramatic moment. It came through years of playing against older athletes, finding ways to contribute, recovering from setbacks and continuing to improve. The young Sabrina Ionescu who had to recruit girls just to form a school team eventually became one of the defining players of her generation. So here I am, singing for you and singing for me, singing life!â She concluded, âThank you so very much for your support and your patience, and if I may say so: I am everything I am because you loved me. â This was also the singerâs first full concert since she last performed a full set in 2020 during her âCourage Tour.' title: Simone Biles built a custom $3 million waterfront mansion in Texas; after years of planning and delays, the Olympian settled into the lakefront estate following a prior $1.1 million property buy
text: Simone Biles built a custom $3 million waterfront mansion in Texas; after years of planning and delays, the Olympian settled into the lakefront estate following a prior $1.1 million property buy Simone Biles and her husband Jonathan Owens have finally moved into the Texas home they spent years planning and building. The custom lakefront mansion near Houston was completed on November 11, 2025, after the couple began working on its design in 2020. The project took much longer than they first expected, with Biles sharing updates as the house slowly took shape. The seven-time Olympic medalist and Owens chose to build the home from the ground up instead of buying a finished property. The result is a large lakefront house with spaces designed around their everyday life, pets and love of sports. When did Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens start building their Texas mansion The story of Simone Biles and Jonathan Owensâ new home began in 2020, when they started planning the property. Biles later explained that simply getting the design ready took about a year. The next wait came from the homeowners association. According to Biles, the required approvals took time, which pushed the actual start of construction to February 2022. That meant the couple had already spent a long time thinking about the house before construction even began. Once work started, Biles continued to share photos and videos showing the property at different stages, from the early framework to the finished rooms. The house was expected to take far less time. After years of waiting, Biles summed up her frustration in a short Instagram update: "They lied when they said nine months to build!" She also shared the timeline behind the project, writing: "Home building requires a lot of patience." Biles later explained: "Started the design process in 2020 and took a year to complete," before adding, "Approvals took a while from [the] HOA; broke ground in Feb 2022; completed 11/11/25." The project therefore stretched across several major moments in the couple's lives. They got married in 2023, while Biles also returned to competition and competed at the Paris Olympics in 2024. What is inside Simone Biles and Jonathan Owensâ $3 million lakefront home The home was built around a mix of comfort, entertainment and spaces that fit the couple's interests. The property has been widely estimated at around $3 million, although the exact final cost has not been publicly confirmed. One of the main features is the kitchen. It has two large islands, custom cabinets and black-and-white marble details. Large glass doors also connect the living areas with the outdoor space and lake views. The house also has a primary bathroom with a large marble finish, two sinks and a spacious shower. There is a game room, home theater and wet bar, giving the couple several areas to spend time at home. Sports are also part of the property. The outdoor area includes a swimming pool and spa beside the lake, along with a basketball court. An in-ground trampoline has also been built close to the water. The house has several personal touches that make it different from a standard luxury property. Biles and Owens have a separate room for their dogs, complete with a pet spa area and built-in feeding space. The room uses the same black-and-white look seen in other parts of the house. The laundry room is another detail Biles has highlighted. Instead of sharing one set of machines, the couple have separate washers and dryers. Biles joked about the reason behind that decision, writing: "Since Jonathan always wants to do laundry the exact same day as me," and then adding, "Now [there is] one set for each of us." How did Simone Bilesâ earlier $1.1 million Texas property compare with the new mansion Before the lakefront house was completed, Biles already had a Texas home where she and Owens spent time during the construction period. Realtor.com reported in 2024 that Biles bought the contemporary Spring, Texas, property in 2020. The 4,000-square-foot home has four bedrooms and 3.5 bathrooms and sits on just over an acre. The property had been listed for $863,500 in 2020, but the exact amount Biles paid was not publicly confirmed. That makes the often-repeated $1.1 million purchase figure difficult to verify. The earlier home also had several features that suited Biles' lifestyle, including a large kitchen, open living areas, a primary suite and a mud room with a pet-washing and feeding area. It also appeared in the Netflix documentary series âSimone Biles Rising,â which followed the gymnast's life and return to elite competition. The new lakefront property is a different kind of home. Rather than taking an existing house and adapting it, Biles and Owens had the chance to decide what they wanted from the beginning. That included the layout, sports areas, pet space and entertainment rooms. When did Simone Biles and Jonathan Owens finally move into the new Texas home The house was officially completed in November 2025, but the couple did not immediately settle into it full time. At the time, Jonathan Owens was playing for the Chicago Bears, meaning the couple spent part of their time in Chicago. After the NFL season ended, Biles began sharing more pictures from the Texas property as the couple started making the house their home. title: After Olympic glory, Manu Bhaker chases the one medal missing from her collection at Asian Games
text: Manu Bhaker PUNE: There is something about Manu Bhaker . Her Serbian coach, Jelena Arunovic, feels Manuâs presence in the field is not just defined by her achievements. âI think an athlete is defined not just by achievements, but also by longevity. If someone has been competing at the highest level for almost 10 years, regularly reaching finals and standing on international podiums, I donât think there is a better rÃ©sume than that,â the Olympic gold-winning coach told TOI. text: Photo: @yaylagulramazanova/ Instagram The Olympics often bring us some dramatic breakthroughs that leave behind a trail of inspirational stories, but only a few as unusual as this one. At the Paris 2024 Games, Azerbaijani archer Yaylagul Ramazanova stepped onto the field six and a half months pregnant, competing against rivals half her age and twice her experience. What happened next turned her into an unlikely fan favorite. Down to the wire in a tiebreaker against a heavily experienced Chinese opponent, Ramazanova felt something unexpected, and what happened next was anything but ordinary. Her story is no less miraculous, almost like a blessing from above. Letâs dig in to find out who she is and what her story is about. Who is Yaylagul Ramazanova Yaylagul Ramazanova is an archer from Azerbaijan who made headlines at the Paris 2024 Olympics. At 34, she competed at the games while being six and a half months pregnant, becoming only the second archer from her country ever to reach the platform. Ramazanova actually started out as a shooter before switching to archery, after a coach noticed her long arms might suit the sport better. Her story at the games became an example of motherhood and the bond a mother and baby share with each other even before the child is born in the world. Ramazanovaâs baby kicked, and she hit a perfect score Ramazanova, 34, was competing in her first Olympics, but her toughest test came early, in the women's individual elimination round against China's An Qixuan, an archer who had entered the match as the favourite. The two were locked at 5-5, forcing a tiebreaker where each competitor gets just one arrow to decide the outcome. That's when Ramazanova says her baby stepped in. "I felt my baby kick me before I shot this last arrow, and then I shot a 10," Ramazanova told Chinese state news agency Xinhua News. While An Qixuan scored a 9, Ramazanova's perfect shot sent her through to the round of 16 of the games. She trained throughout her pregnancy Ramazanova, who initially competed in shooting before switching to archery, said she never saw her pregnancy as something working against her during preparation for the Games. Instead, she described it as a source of strength. "I didn't feel uncomfortable with my pregnancy," Ramazanova said to Xinhua News. title: Meet Cameron Myers, the 20-year-old Australian who beat two Olympic champions to win the Diamond League 1,500m final in 3:30.14
text: Cameron Myers, the 20-year-old Australian who beat two Olympic champions to win the Diamond League At just 20, Australian middle-distance runner Cameron Myers has produced the biggest victory of his young career, winning the men's 1,500 metres at the 2026 Diamond League Final in Brussels. Myers clocked 3:30.14, edging Kenya's Phanuel Kipkosgei Koech by just 0.04 seconds in a dramatic finish. According to Reuters and Adelaide Now, Myers overcame a field packed with some of the world's leading middle-distance runners, including the two most recent Olympic champions in the event, American Cole Hocker and Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen. Hocker finished seventh in 3:30.80, while Ingebrigtsen placed fourth in 3:30.52. The victory made Myers only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League Final and capped a breakthrough season in which he has established himself as one of the country's most promising middle-distance athletes. A dramatic finish in Brussels The men's 1,500m final brought together a remarkably strong field, with Olympic champions, international medal contenders and several of the world's fastest runners lining up in Brussels. Myers entered the race as one of Australia's rising stars, but the quality of the field presented an enormous challenge. The race remained tightly contested through the final stages. Myers positioned himself within striking distance before making his decisive move in the home straight. That strategy paid off. Myers produced a powerful finishing kick to overtake the runners around him and narrowly beat Koech to the line. Myers finished in 3:30.14, Koech in 3:30.18 and American Ethan Strand in 3:30.50. Ingebrigtsen followed in fourth with 3:30.52, while Yared Nuguse, Hobbs Kessler and Hocker completed the next three places. The margin between first and second was only four hundredths of a second, highlighting just how close the race became in its final metres. Myers' rapid rise The Brussels victory did not come out of nowhere. Myers has been building an impressive rÃ©sumÃ© throughout 2026 and has steadily established himself among the world's elite 1,500m runners. One defining moment of his season came in June at the Paris Diamond League meeting, where he ran 3:28.00 to set an Australian national record. That performance also ranked among the fastest 1,500m times in the world this year. He later won the mile at the Prefontaine Classic in Eugene, recording 3:46.06. Myers also earned a silver medal in the mile at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, finishing behind Scottish world-record holder Josh Kerr. Just days before the Diamond League Final, he won the 1,500m at the ISTAF meeting in Berlin in 3:30.96. His consistency across different competitions has helped transform him from a promising young Australian runner into a serious international contender. Beating Olympic champions What made the Brussels victory particularly significant was the strength of the athletes Myers defeated. Ingebrigtsen won the Olympic 1,500m title at the Tokyo Games, while Hocker captured Olympic gold in the event at Paris 2024. Both were expected to be major contenders in Brussels, yet neither finished on the podium. Ingebrigtsen crossed the line fourth in 3:30.52, while Hocker finished seventh in 3:30.80. The result demonstrated that Myers could compete successfully against established champions rather than simply winning when the biggest names were absent. The Australian's victory also came in a race where the top seven runners all finished within less than a second of one another, making his ability to time his final acceleration particularly important. A new chapter for Australian athletics Myers' Diamond League triumph represents another important milestone for Australian middle-distance running. The official Diamond League profile now lists him as a Diamond League Final winner and records his personal best of 3:28.00 in the 1,500m. The 20-year-old's rise has been especially notable due to his rapid progression. His national record in Paris, international victories and Commonwealth Games medals have all come in a single breakthrough season. His Brussels victory now adds one of the sport's most prestigious annual titles to that record. More importantly, beating two Olympic champions in a tightly fought final suggests Myers is no longer simply viewed as Australia's next big middle-distance prospect. He has already shown that he can deliver when competing against the best in the world, and at only 20, he may have several more years to build on that breakthrough. text: Inspiring story of the day: âHaving a dad with a big name doesnât do the work for youâ - How Trinity Rodman rose above Dennis Rodmanâs shadow, lived in motels, and built her own soccer legacy Trinity Rodman has built a soccer career that now stands on its own. The Washington Spirit star is a 2024 Olympic gold medalist, a 2021 NWSL champion and, as of January 2026, the highest-paid player in NWSL history. But her childhood looked very different from what many people expected from the daughter of NBA legend Dennis Rodman . Trinity and her brother DJ once lived with their mother, Michelle Moyer, in a Ford Expedition and cheap motels in Newport Beach. Through those difficult years, Michelle kept life feeling normal for her children. That bond helped shape Trinity into the player she is today. How did Trinity Rodman live in a car despite being Dennis Rodmanâs daughter Having a famous father did not mean Trinity Rodman grew up with an easy life. After Dennis Rodman and Michelle Moyer separated, Trinity, her brother DJ and their mother faced serious money problems. For a period, they moved between a Ford Expedition and motels when Michelle could afford a room. The situation was especially strange because they were living in Newport Beach, where Trinity went to a wealthy school. She has spoken about seeing classmates arrive in expensive cars while her own family was trying to work out where they would stay. On Call Her Daddy , Trinity explained just how unusual those years were: âWe had a Ford Expedition and we lived in that for a little bit. Mind you, in Newport Beachâ¦ So imagine living in a car going to a rich school when everybody else is in Rolls-Royces and Range Rovers. But my mom tried to make every situation seem smoother than it actually was. title: One Tech Tip: How to avoid Celine Dion ticket scams as she makes her grand concert comeback
text: Celine Dion Based on their experience of hosting Taylor Swift, the management team at the Paris venue for Celine Dion 's grand concert comeback is bracing to deliver devastating news to hundreds of her fans: 'Sorry, you appear to have been scammed, your tickets are fake. ' The Grammy-winning star's long-awaited return to the concert stage after years away from touring has unleashed massive pent-up demand for tickets. It's a perfect storm for scammers who have wormed their way into fans' online communities and set up fraudulent ticketing websites to manipulate and rob fans of both their money and hopes of being able to say, "I was there." "Where there is massive demand and widespread excitement, fraudsters see a golden opportunity," says Group-IB, a Singapore-based cybersecurity firm that works with the international police agency Interpol and others. The first of the 26 shows is Saturday. Here are some tips to avoid the traps: For the few tickets left, use only authorized sites The Plenitude Arena, hosting Dion for 16 dates in September and October and another 10 in May, says the highest risk of scams is when tickets first go on sale - which was April for the upcoming concerts and June for the 2027 series - and in the shows' immediate build-up. "That's when the public will be very exposed to these scammers," Celine Trioux, the arena's marketing director, said in an Associated Press interview. "People are going to wake up and think, 'Oh, right, I didn't get a ticket, everyone is going, I want to go,' or 'I've seen the first show all over social media, it looks amazing, I'm going to find a ticket by any means possible.' And that's also when the scammers will be out in force." The shows sold out immediately, although a few VIP packages with Champagne and other perks are still available for between 1,099 euros and 2,990 euros (US$1,276 and $3,473) on the arena's website. One other possibility is to buy tickets from people who no longer want theirs. But the only way to do that safely is on three sites that are authorized for resales: AXS France, Ticketmaster France and Fnac Spectacles, Trioux said. There are unlikely to be many of those. Generally, just 4% to 8% of people who buy tickets for the arena end up not wanting or not being able to use them. "I strongly advise against buying a ticket from an individual or from someone advertising it on social media, because there's no way to know whether it's genuine or whether the same ticket will also be sold to other people," Trioux said. Check URLs to avoid fraudulent sites Group-IB says it found an array of fraudulent websites that impersonated official ticketing platforms as well as the official sites for Dion and for the arena. Some URL web addresses were close to the real thing, like celinedion.co (instead of celinedion.com), ticketmaster-celinedion.fr (instead of ticketmaster.fr ) or axs-billetterie.com (instead of axs.com ). "The first reflex should always be to check the website's URL," Trioux said. She said lawyers identified nearly 200 fraudulent Dion-related sites and social media accounts that offered tickets but that "when we shut down one copycat website, another one opens." "It's a constant battle," Trioux added. "It's impossible to close them all because technology is advancing faster than legal authorities can act." The Paris concert section of Dion's site has clickable links to all of the authorized ticket sellers. The arena says it will help fraud victims Group-IB says fraudsters appear to have reused scamming tools that were also deployed to target Oasis fans when the Britpop band reunited for a tour in 2025 and during Swift's 2023-2024 Eras tour. When Swift played four Paris shows in 2024, the Plenitude Arena had to turn away about "400 to 500 people who had been duped," Trioux said. She said that for Dion, the arena is expecting possibly hundreds of fraud victims each night. The concert series is a major milestone for the 58-year-old Quebec-born singer, her first since she revealed in 2022 her diagnosis with stiff-person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder. She last performed briefly in Paris at the opening ceremony of the Olympic Games in 2024, wowing with "Hymne a l'amour" (Hymn to love) from atop the Eiffel Tower in the rain. Fans are traveling from far afield to reconnect with one of the most decorated artists in pop music history. For those who have been scammed, the shock could be brutal. "We'll have a complaints desk for all these people, because they will generally discover the problem at the entrance, when they present their fake ticket," Trioux said. "Staff will be there to receive them and explain the procedure to follow if they wish to file a police complaint." Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

text: Who are Qinwen Zhengâs parents? Meet Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang, the people behind her tennis journey Qinwen Zhengâs rise in tennis has been closely linked to the support of her parents, Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang. The Chinese star was born in Shiyan, Hubei, and started playing sports as a young child before tennis became her main focus. Her parents soon realized that she had the talent and drive to go further. From changing cities for better coaching to making major personal sacrifices, they played a big role in her journey. Who are Qinwen Zhengâs parents, Zheng Jianping and Deng Fang? Qinwenâs father, Zheng Jianping, had a sporting background of his own. He competed in track and field events in Hubei and was part of the provinceâs second-level track team during his high school years. After leaving sports, he moved into business and later ran an auto parts company in Shiyan that dealt with cars, steel and construction materials. His own experience in sports helped him understand the hard work needed to compete at a high level. When Qinwen was young, Jianping encouraged her to try different sports. A moment when she chose to run instead of taking a ride in the family car helped him notice how much she enjoyed physical activity. Tennis eventually became the sport she wanted to pursue. Qinwenâs mother, Deng Fang, came from a very different work background. She studied railway transport and worked at railway stations in Hubei, including jobs involving ticket sales. Her role later changed when Qinwenâs tennis career became more demanding. Deng left her job so she could spend more time with her daughter and take care of her during training and travel. The two parents supported Qinwen in different ways. Her father focused heavily on her tennis development and the decisions around her career, while her mother handled much of the daily care. Qinwen has spoken about how important both parents have been to her success. Qinwen Zhengâs tennis journey and how her parents supported her Qinwen was born on October 8, 2002, in Shiyan, Hubei. She began playing tennis locally when she was six, but her parents soon understood that she would need better coaching to develop properly. When she was eight, the family moved her to Wuhan, around 200 kilometers away, where she trained for several years. Her next move was to Beijing, where she received more advanced training. Then, at 17, Qinwen moved to Barcelona with her mother to continue her development and compete in Europe. By then, tennis had become a full-time commitment, and her family had built their lives around giving her the best chance to succeed. That path also came with a major financial cost. Qinwen has said her father made huge sacrifices to keep paying for her career, including selling the family home. Some reports have put the total amount spent on her development at around 20 million yuan, although that figure has not been independently confirmed. Dengâs sacrifice was just as important in a different way. After leaving her railway job, she stayed close to Qinwen and helped manage the everyday parts of her life, from meals and travel to making sure she had support away from the court. Qinwen has never hidden how much she values what her parents did for her. After winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024, she credited them for helping her reach that level. Their approach was demanding, but it gave her the chance to build a career on her own terms. title: Trinity Rodman's US Open moment reveals an old habit in sports broadcasting: introducing women by their relationships first
text: Ben Shelton and Trinity Rodman. Image via: Getty Images Trinity Rodman was sitting in Ben Shelton's player box at the US Open on Tuesday when the cameras found her. The ESPN commentary that followed introduced her as âTrinity Rodman, also known as Ben Shelton's girlfriend, and also known as a member of the US women's national team.â The on-screen graphic was similarly arranged: âBen's girlfriend & USWNT player. â Rodman is, of course, Shelton's girlfriend. The two tennis and football stars made their relationship public in March 2025, after Rodman slid into Shelton's DMs. Shelton, 23, is one of American tennis's leading players, a left-handed power hitter who reached a career-high world No.5 in late 2025 and has already won four ATP titles in 2026, including the National Bank Open two weeks before the US Open. But Rodman has spent the better part of her career becoming recognisable without him. The 24-year-old is an Olympic gold medallist, an NWSL champion and the highest-paid women's footballer in the world. She is also the daughter of NBA Hall of Famer Dennis Rodman, another fact that has often followed her into introductions of her own. Soccer player Trinity Rodman celebrates after her boyfriend Ben Shelton, of the United States, won his match against Hubert Hurkacz, of Poland, during the second round of the U.S. Open tennis championships Wednesday, Sept. 2, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth) The ESPN description prompted a familiar reaction from fans online, particularly because there was no shortage of things from Rodman's own career that could have been used instead. âGeezâ¦ she is so much more than Ben's girlfriend,â one fan wrote. Another put it more bluntly: âTrin is an Olympic gold medalist, NWSL player and then Ben's girlfriend. In that order.â Rodman's career does not need Shelton's name attached to it Rodman's football career began long before she became a fixture in Shelton's box. The Washington Spirit selected her No.2 overall in the 2021 NWSL Draft when she was 18, making her the youngest player ever selected at the time. She won the league's Rookie of the Year award and helped Washington win the NWSL Championship in her first season. Three years later, she produced one of the defining moments of her international career. In the 2024 Paris Olympics final, Rodman scored in extra time against Japan as the United States won women's football gold for the first time since 2012. She now has 13 goals in 57 appearances for the USWNT. At club level, her value has grown just as quickly. Rodman became the first player signed under the NWSL's High Impact Player rule and agreed a landmark deal with Washington worth more than $1 million per season through 2028, making her the highest-paid player in the league. FILE - Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman in action during the second half of an NWSL soccer match against the Portland Thorns FC, Friday, March 13, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Terrance Williams,File) There is also the question of her surname, which has brought its own assumptions. Rodman has spoken openly about her complicated relationship with her father and rejected the idea that the name defines her. âHeâs not a dad. Maybe by blood, but nothing else,â she said on Call Her Daddy . âI love to have my last name and when I say Rodman, itâs not my dadâs name, itâs my name.â She has been less defensive about being known as Shelton's partner. In fact, Rodman has said she actually likes the term WAG , even while acknowledging why some people dislike it. âFor me, I think I like the term personally because, like I said before, I feel like 24/7 I'm on in front of cameras, and so I think I use the term WAG for me to simplify what I'm doing,â she said on Not Gonna Lie with Kylie Kelce in August. âFor me, saying WAG, it's me being like, âI'm Ben's girlfriend.â But I can understand why it's so hated.â She described being able to share that experience with Shelton as âthe best feeling in the worldâ, pointing to the fact that both are constantly training, competing and exhausting themselves doing the sports they love. That distinction matters. Rodman choosing to embrace the label is not the same thing as it being the most useful way to introduce her. This has happened before The US Open moment was not the first time Rodman's identity has been filtered through the people around her. At Wimbledon in 2025, she was introduced during one of Shelton's matches as âTiffanyâ and had her father mentioned in the same breath. This time, the mistake was different. Her name was right, her relationship was real and her football career was acknowledged. Yet the order still said something: Ben's girlfriend first, USWNT player second. Washington Spirit forward Trinity Rodman shoots as Seattle Reign FC midfielder Samantha Meza, right, looks on during the first half of an NWSL soccer match, Sunday, May 10, 2026, in Seattle. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson) There was plenty of room for a different introduction. Rodman was not simply another celebrity sitting in a tennis player's box. She was an Olympic champion watching another elite American athlete compete at one of the biggest sporting events in the world. She can be Dennis Rodman's daughter. She can even happily call herself a WAG. None of those things requires her own achievements to come second. At 24, Trinity Rodman has already built a career substantial enough to stand on its own. At the US Open, she happened to be there to support someone else. title: Neeraj Chopraâs injury battles: From elbow surgery in 2019 to an ankle ligament tear in 2026 - the setbacks and comebacks that defined his career
text: Neeraj Chopraâs injury battles Neeraj Chopraâs career has been defined by historic throws, Olympic medals and a relentless pursuit of excellence. But alongside those milestones has been a recurring challenge: injuries that have repeatedly interrupted his season. Neeraj Chopra has been ruled out of the 2026 Asian Games and the remainder of the season after suffering an ankle ligament tear during training. The injury comes just days after he finished second at the Lausanne Diamond League with a season-best 88.05m. It is another frustrating setback for the two-time Olympic medallist, who had only recently returned from a lengthy injury layoff. Here is a look at the major injury setbacks that have disrupted his career. 2026: An ankle tear ends his season Chopra's latest injury is an ankle ligament tear sustained during training. The injury rules him out of the Asian Games, the Diamond League Final and the World Athletics Ultimate Championships, bringing his 2026 campaign to an early end. It comes after a promising return to competition following almost nine months away from the sport. Neeraj Chopra (PTI Photo) 2025-26: A long road back from a back injury Chopra's previous major setback came with a back injury that kept him away from competition for around nine months. He had competed at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo despite carrying the problem, finishing eighth. The injury subsequently forced him into an extended rehabilitation period. His comeback was delayed further in 2026, with Chopra missing the Doha Diamond League before eventually returning to competitive action. 2024: Adductor concerns before Paris The 2024 season brought another fitness scare. Chopra withdrew from the Ostrava Golden Spike after experiencing discomfort in his adductor. Chopra subsequently opted out of the Paris Diamond League, again because of his troublesome adductor/groin issue. He later explained that he did not want to take unnecessary risks with the Paris Olympics approaching. The decision paid off as Chopra stayed fit for the Olympics and successfully defended his place on the podium, winning silver in Paris. title: A 16-year interlude: Shannon Rowburyâs wait for Olympic justice & her medal
text: Shannon Rowbury KOLKATA: For Shannon Rowbury, the 2012 London Olympics never really ended. The US middle-distance runner finished sixth in the womenâs 1500m final that night, believing she had missed out on an Olympic medal. But what followed over the next 13 years was the unravelling of one of the most tainted races in Olympic history. Turkeyâs Asli Cakir Alptekin and Gamze Bulut, who finished first and second respectively, were later disqualified for doping. Russiaâs Tatyana Tomashova, who was initially fourth and subsequently promoted to silver, was also disqualified following a doping case in 2024. As a result, Rowbury was eventually elevated to third. In June 2025, IOC officially reallocated the medals, making Rowbury the 2012 Olympic 1500m bronze medallist. Now, 16 years after the London race, the American will finally receive the medal physically at Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 â in front of the people who matter most to her. âIâm an optimistic person, so I always try to find the silver linings,â Rowbury said in Bhubaneswar last month. âItâs been a very difficult thing. When I found out the news, my entire body started shaking. I started sobbing. It was so much of the frustration I had carried within me about the unfairness of sport.â The London 1500m final has since become infamous, with six of the top nine finishers either disqualified or linked to performance-enhancing drug use. For Rowbury, however, the story is no longer simply about what she lost in London. It is about what clean sport ultimately gave her back. âI try to have gratitude for the fact that I do get justice in my story,â she said. âI will now have the opportunity to receive my medal in front of my two children. They will see their mother being recognised for winning with integrity, winning the right way.â That sense of justice has also shaped what Rowbury does today. She works with US Anti-Doping and speaks at conferences and events, trying to bring a human dimension to the fight against doping. Asked about Indiaâs doping problem and what federations can do to bring down the numbers, Rowbury stressed that the answer cannot be limited to testing and punishment. âItâs not just about winning a race; itâs about sportsmanship and how you win,â she said, arguing for an ecosystem that encourages performance while making it clear that cheating carries consequences. âOnce there is a clear directive that if you are cheating and you are caught, that you will miss your eligibility or there will be penalties, then hopefully that will disincentivise that performance.â But Rowbury also believes the solution needs to begin much earlier, during the development of young athletes and the creation of strong foundations built around the right values. Her own experience has also changed the way she looks at athletes â and perhaps explains why her transition into broadcasting has felt so natural. Rowbury began broadcasting while she was still competing, covering smaller meets in 2017 before retiring from competition in 2021. She has since worked in various roles with USA Track & Field, World Athletics and several broadcasters, and won an Emmy for her work during the Paris Olympics. That understanding has followed her to India, where she recently visited for the World Athletics Silver Level Continental Tour and worked on in-stadium commentary while also conducting a workshop for aspiring Indian broadcasters. But it is Los Angeles that now looms large in her mind. When Rowbury walks into an Olympic stadium in 2028, she will not be chasing another medal. title: Jemele Hill slams âjealous of Caitlinâ narrative as Enes Kanter Freedom targets Indiana Fever
text: Jemele Hill slams âjealous of Caitlinâ narrative as Enes Kanter Freedom targets Indiana Fever Jemele Hill has challenged the growing media narrative around Caitlin Clark after the three-time WNBA All-Star made her senior national team debut against China at the FIBA Womenâs Basketball World Cup. Hill argued that repeated claims of players being jealous of Clark carry racial undertones that are often ignored. Her comments came after Linda Cohn questioned Aâja Wilsonâs decision to withdraw from the tournament despite Team USA citing health concerns. Meanwhile, former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom has created another WNBA controversy by saying he wants the Indiana Fever to draft him in 2027 so he can play alongside Clark. Jemele Hill questions Linda Cohnâs comments about Aâja Wilson Hill addressed the issue in a Saturday thread, arguing that major media personalities can make strong claims about the WNBA without receiving enough pushback. She specifically pointed toward the repeated idea that other WNBA players are jealous of Caitlin Clark, saying the discussion has a racial element that deserves more attention. Hill wrote: âSo when people with big microphones start chiming in on the W and offering silly opinions, there isn't a lot of pushback or counter narratives. There's also the issue of race. This whole everybody is jealous of Caitlin Clark narrative has such obvious racial undertones. I promise you if the league were 70 percent white instead of Black, this would never be said.â Her comments followed criticism of former ESPN anchor Linda Cohn, who questioned why Aâja Wilson was not playing alongside Clark for Team USA. Wilson withdrew from the World Cup shortly before the tournament, with health concerns given as the reason for her absence. Cohn nevertheless wondered whether Wilson might have been uncomfortable with the attention surrounding Clark and questioned whether insecurity had influenced her decision. Cohn even imagined what Wilson could have been thinking, saying: âCould she be thinking, âI'm the four-time MVP, I'm the best player in the world. Why does everything have to be about Caitlin Clark?ââ Those comments quickly became a major talking point among WNBA fans and drew criticism from several prominent figures. Hill believes the focus on supposed jealousy takes attention away from what the players actually do on the court. For Hill, the bigger concern is that this type of speculation can deepen divisions among fans instead of encouraging meaningful discussion about basketball. She argued that WNBA players are elite competitors and deserve analysis based on their performances rather than assumptions about their personal feelings toward Clark. The debate comes as Clark begins another important chapter with Team USA. After missing the 2024 Paris Olympics, the Indiana Fever star finally made her senior national team debut at the World Cup, adding another major moment to her rapidly growing career. Enes Kanter Freedom wants Indiana Fever to draft him alongside Caitlin Clark While Hill was criticizing the conversation around Clark, former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom created another unusual WNBA storyline. Freedom has publicly said he intends to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft, despite league sources reportedly making clear that he does not meet the eligibility requirements. title: Novak Djokovic injuries: How every painful setback tested the tennis star, yet he rose each time to fight his way back
text: Novak Djokovic injuries: How every painful setback tested the tennis star, yet he rose each time to fight his way back â¢;Novak Djokovicâs career has had almost everything a tennis player can face physically, from breathing problems and heat illness to serious elbow, shoulder, abdominal, hamstring and knee injuries. Some forced him to stop matches, while others came during Grand Slam runs. Yet Djokovic kept finding ways back. Even in 2026, after another difficult physical battle at the US Open, he is still competing at the highest level. Novak Djokovicâs major injuries and how he fought through them â¢ 2005 French Open: Djokovic retired against Guillermo Coria with a lower-back injury. â¢ 2006 French Open: He stopped against Rafael Nadal because of a back and thigh problem. â¢ 2007 Wimbledon: A badly infected blister on his left toe, along with back and overall physical problems, forced him to retire against Nadal in the semifinals. Djokovic later said he did not want to make the injury worse. â¢ 2009 Australian Open: Djokovic retired against Andy Roddick after struggling with heat illness, cramps and soreness in extreme conditions. â¢ 2010â11 health struggles: Djokovic had repeated breathing and energy problems during matches. He later changed his diet after identifying a sensitivity to gluten, which he credited with helping him feel stronger and more comfortable on court. â¢ 2016â18 right elbow injury: The elbow problem became a major setback and ended his 2017 season after Wimbledon. He had surgery in January 2018. Months later, he won Wimbledon and the US Open and finished the year as world No. 1. â¢ 2019 US Open: A left shoulder injury forced Djokovic to retire against Stan Wawrinka while trailing 6-4, 7-5, 2-1. â¢ 2021 Australian Open: Djokovic suffered an abdominal muscle tear during his match with Taylor Fritz but continued the tournament and won the title. â¢ 2023 Australian Open: He arrived with a left hamstring injury and needed heavy strapping and medical treatment during early rounds. He still defeated Stefanos Tsitsipas in the final to win his 10th Australian Open title. â¢ 2024 French Open: Djokovic tore the meniscus in his right knee during his fourth-round win over Francisco CerÃºndolo. He withdrew from the tournament and had surgery. Just over eight weeks later, he won Olympic gold in Paris after beating Carlos Alcaraz. â¢ 2025: A continuing shoulder injury eventually forced Djokovic to withdraw from the ATP Finals after he had won the Athens title. â¢ 2026 US Open: Djokovic faced another physical test against Mariano Navone. He dealt with vomiting, cramps, back and shoulder pain during a four-hour, 36-minute first-round match before losing in five sets. Novak Djokovicâs recent injuries show the same fight The 2026 US Open loss was very different from some of Djokovicâs famous injury comebacks because this time he could not find a way through. Still, the match showed why his physical struggles have become such an important part of his story. He had already dealt with health problems during the season, yet continued to compete. That attitude was clear after his 2024 knee surgery too. Djokovic did not simply return to tennis; he pushed himself back into Grand Slam and Olympic competition. He reached the Wimbledon final and then won Olympic gold only weeks after the operation. title: Celine Dion makes a rare appearance in Paris ahead of the 26th residency show, which marks her much-awaited musical return after 2022 Stiff-Person Syndrome diagnosis
