title: From Anaya Bangarâs cricket return to Imane Khelifâs Olympic gold controversy: The biggest transgender and gender-eligibility debates in sport
text: The biggest transgender and gender-eligibility debates in sport (Agency Images) NEW DELHI: Anaya Bangar's return to cricket has opened a much bigger conversation about transgender athletes in sport, one that now extends far beyond the cricket field. The former Mumbai Under-19 cricketer has received clearance from Cricket Australia to play women's community cricket in the country, giving her a route back into competitive cricket after beginning her transition in 2022. Bangar can participate in Premier Cricket, which Cricket Australia classifies as community cricket, immediately. Her pathway to elite cricket from March 2027, however, comes with eligibility conditions, including a requirement to provide a blood test confirming that her serum testosterone remains below the prescribed threshold and that she continues to meet the governing body's policy requirements. Anaya Bangar returns to cricket The decision has already divided opinion. South Africa all-rounder Marizanne Kapp publicly criticised Cricket Australia's position, describing the decision as "absolutely ridiculous" and arguing against transgender women competing in women's cricket. Bangar's case is therefore not simply about one cricketer. The Olympics have taken a very different route Laurel Hubbard: the Olympic milestone Few athletes illustrate that change more clearly than New Zealand weightlifter Laurel Hubbard. Hubbard became the first openly transgender woman to compete at an Olympic Games when she took part in the women's super-heavyweight weightlifting competition at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. She did not complete a successful lift in the competition and finished without a result. At the time, her participation was viewed as a landmark moment for transgender representation in elite sport. Five years later, the IOC has adopted a fundamentally different approach. From Los Angeles 2028, transgender women who do not satisfy the IOC's biological-sex eligibility requirements will not be eligible for the women's category at the Games. Lia Thomas and the battle that changed American college sport In the United States, swimmer Lia Thomas became one of the most prominent figures in the debate. Thomas competed for the University of Pennsylvania after transitioning and became the first openly transgender athlete to win an NCAA Division I individual title when she won the women's 500-yard freestyle in 2022. Her participation triggered intense debate over eligibility, fairness and the rules governing transgender athletes in collegiate sport. The issue has since moved well beyond one swimmer. In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that laws in West Virginia and Idaho restricting transgender athletes from participating on female school and college teams did not violate Title IX. The court's decision cleared the way for states to maintain such restrictions based on biological sex. Emily Bridges and the battle over cycling Emily Bridges. (Twitter Photo) Cycling produced another highly visible case through British rider Emily Bridges. Bridges, who had previously competed in men's cycling, sought to compete in women's events after transitioning. Her eligibility became the subject of intense debate in 2022 when she was ruled ineligible for the women's event at the British National Omnium Championships. The wider issue eventually contributed to a significant change in international cycling policy. The Union Cycliste Internationale, cycling's world governing body, changed its rules in 2023 and prohibited transgender women who transitioned after male puberty from competing in women's events on its international calendar. The organisation said its decision was based on the available scientific evidence and the need to protect equal opportunities in the women's category. Imane Khelif: The boxing controversy that blurred the lines Imane Khelif (Image Via Getty) The transgender debate in sport is also frequently linked to another high-profile case, but Imane Khelif's story needs to be treated separately. Khelif is not a transgender athlete. The Algerian boxer was born and raised as a woman and competed in the women's 66kg category at the Paris 2024 Olympics, where she went on to win the gold medal. Yet her participation became one of the biggest controversies of the Games. The issue stemmed from a dispute between boxing's governing bodies. The International Boxing Association (IBA) said Khelif had failed its eligibility requirements at the 2023 World Championships and claimed that testing had found her ineligible to compete in the women's category. However, the IBA did not publicly release the underlying test results. The IOC, which was responsible for the boxing competition at Paris 2024, rejected the IBA's position and allowed Khelif to compete. Indiana Fever player Sophie Cunningham recently reignited the debate after speaking publicly about transgender participation in women's sport. Her comments generated both support and criticism, forcing the WNBA to address an issue that had largely remained outside the league's immediate competitive spotlight. WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert subsequently told teams that the league would continue discussing transgender participation, acknowledging the growing attention surrounding the issue. The situation is particularly interesting because there is currently no openly transgender player competing in the WNBA. title: India wants more Olympic medals but 'doesn't participate in half the sports'; PM Modi speaks out 'bitter truth'
text: Prime Minister Narendra Modi NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday said India cannot expect a significant rise in its Olympic medal tally unless it starts competing in many sports where it currently has little or no representation, including surfing and sport climbing. Addressing athletes, students and volunteers virtually during the Khelo India Dialogue ahead of National Sports Day on August 29, PM Modi said India's sports vision is not just about winning medals but also about making sports a part of nation-building. Sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya joined the event virtually from IIT Gandhinagar. Prime Minister Modi pointed out that India still does not compete in many Olympic sports. "In the Olympics, there are so many different sports... Indian teams don't even participate in half of them, which means that we are not competing for a major chunk of the medal tally," Modi said, calling it a "bitter truth". He said this has been the situation for many years. "And this has been going on for decades. In 2012, we competed in only 13 sports. We were not even there in over 20 events and not many in the country even knew about some of these competitions. "Other countries win medals in those sports, and we don't even participate. To increase our medals, we have to improve in these sports," he pointed out. India participated in 16 of the 32 sports at the 2024 Paris Olympics. PM Modi specifically mentioned surfing and sport climbing, two sports that are part of the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics but have never seen an Indian competitor. title: Alexander Zverev vs Daniil Medvedev: Who is richer? Career earnings, brand deals, lifestyle
text: Alexander Zverev and Daniil Medvedev (Getty Images) Alexander Zverev and Daniil Medvedev are two of the biggest names tennis has produced after the Federer-Nadal-Djokovic era. Both have won Grand Slams, both have spent years inside the world's top five, and both base themselves in Monaco. On the surface, they look like peers. But the financial gap between them is far wider than their on-court rivalry suggests. Prize money, endorsement pull, and one unforgettable afternoon on the Paris clay in 2026 have quietly pushed Zverev into a different bracket altogether. Alexander Zverev vs Daniil Medvedev net worth comparison in 2026 According to Celebrity Net Worth, Alexander Zverev carries a net worth of $40 million, while Daniil Medvedev sits at $20 million. So, the short answer is that Zverev is twice as wealthy as Medvedev, and the reasons go beyond just winning more matches. Zverev's 2026 French Open title pushed his official ATP career prize money to $65,845,262, lifting him to fifth on the all-time men's earnings list -- sitting right behind Federer, Nadal, Djokovic and Sinner. That jump alone tells you how significant one Grand Slam victory can be, not just for legacy, but for the bank account. Medvedev has accumulated approximately $52,323,854 in career prize money, which places him eighth on the same list. Impressive on its own, but Zverev now sits almost $16 million ahead in pure prize money terms. The difference in net worth runs deeper than match results, though. Medvedev won the 2021 US Open and reached world No. 1 in 2022, yet his overall earnings haven't kept pace with Zverev's. Part of that comes down to endorsement power. Medvedev's brand portfolio includes Lacoste, Tecnifibre racquets, Bovet watches, BMW, Tinkoff Bank, and HyperX gaming. It's a solid list, but largely functional -- each brand fits a specific market, and there's no crossover luxury appeal that drives premium deals. Zverev, by contrast, has built a commercial profile more in line with the sport's top earners, with his Olympic gold medal in Tokyo, multiple Masters 1000 titles, and his French Open win all strengthening his marketability considerably. Alexander Zverev's career earnings and major wins Alexander Zverev's path to $65 million in prize money wasn't linear, and that makes it worth examining closely. He turned professional as a teenager and spent years being one of the best players in the world without a Grand Slam to show for it. He won the ATP Finals in 2018 by defeating Djokovic, claimed Olympic gold in Tokyo in 2021, and collected seven Masters 1000 titles. But the majors kept slipping away. He lost the 2020 US Open final to Dominic Thiem, then the 2024 French Open final to Carlos Alcaraz, then the 2025 Australian Open final to Jannik Sinner. Three Grand Slam finals, three losses. Roland Garros 2026 changed everything. He defeated Flavio Cobolli 6-1, 4-6, 6-4, 6-7(5), 6-1 in a match that lasted over four hours and 16 minutes, making him the first German man to win the French Open since 1937. When match point arrived, Zverev dropped to the clay. That title pushed him ahead of Alcaraz and Sinner on the all-time earnings list -- all still-active players. That's the compounding effect of finally winning a major prize money, ranking points, and endorsement leverage all move at once. Daniil Medvedev's earnings and brand value Daniil Medvedev got to a Grand Slam title faster than Zverev did, but the momentum didn't compound in the same way. His defining win came at the 2021 US Open, where he defeated Novak Djokovic in straight sets, denying Djokovic a calendar-year Grand Slam. It remains one of the more significant results in recent tennis history. He also reached the Australian Open final in back-to-back years and became world No. 1 in 2022 â only the third Russian man to hold that ranking, after Yevgeny Kafelnikov and Marat Safin. But since 2022, Medvedev's trajectory has plateaued relative to the other top players. His best earning year was 2023 at $11.55 million, followed by $6.52 million in 2024. Solid figures, but the absence of additional Grand Slam titles has kept his endorsement ceiling lower than it might otherwise have been. His wife Daria Chernyshkova, a former junior tennis player, also serves as his assistant, helping him manage travel logistics including visas for tournaments. The gap between the two is real and unlikely to narrow quickly unless Medvedev adds more major titles to his name. It isn't a reflection of one being a definitively better player -- it's a reflection of how prize money, grand slam titles, and endorsement deals stack over the course of a long career. title: FIBA Women's World Cup 2026: Team USA hit with major blow involving A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum
text: A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum. Image via: Joe Murphy/ NBAE via Getty Images | Getty Images Team USA's roster for the FIBA Women's World Cup just took a hit. A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum, two of the most decorated names in USA Basketball, will not suit up in Berlin. USA Basketball confirmed the withdrawals in a Monday statement, and the timing could hardly be worse. With the U.S. chasing a fifth straight World Cup gold and a brutal group stage waiting on the other side, losing this much frontcourt firepower forces a scramble nobody wanted. A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum pull out of USA roster A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum are both out of the World Cup for health reasons, USA Basketball announced Monday. Sonia Citron and Kiki Iriafen have already been named as their replacements, and both are in Berlin preparing for the tournament opener against China on Friday. It is a significant loss on paper. Wilson is the reigning MVP of the 2022 World Cup and the 2024 Olympics, and Plum has been one of the program's most reliable bench weapons at both events. Why A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum pulled out Plum's absence linked to a lower leg injury that has bothered her most of the WNBA season. She missed nearly six weeks earlier in the year, returned in August, then saw the injury flare up again after her trade from the Los Angeles Sparks to the Phoenix Mercury. The Mercury has since ruled her out for the rest of the WNBA season too. Wilson's situation is murkier. She has dealt with a back issue that popped up on the injury report twice in the past week, though she still played 30 minutes in her last game before the FIBA break. A source told ESPN she has not been fully healthy for a while and there was concern the World Cup's packed schedule would make things worse. Wilson had already hinted at this balancing act back in July. "I have given it some thought, not going to lie," she told The Dunker Spot, adding that she planned to let her body guide the decision as the moment got closer. Who will replace A'ja Wilson and Kelsey Plum? Team USA turned to two Washington Mystics teammates. Sonia Citron, who is averaging 16.8 points per game this season, steps in as a shooting guard rather than a natural point guard, which was Plum's primary role. Kiki Iriafen, one of the WNBA's better young power forwards, gives the frontcourt some of the depth it loses without Wilson. Iriafen already has international experience with this group, having played for the U.S. at the World Cup qualifying tournament in Puerto Rico back in March. Wilson averaged a double-double in Paris, 18.7 points, 10.2 rebounds and 2.7 blocks a game, and closed the gold medal win over France with 21 points, 13 rebounds and four blocks. title: Inspiring story of the day: âIt made us tougher, it made us more hungry for successâ - How Novak Djokovic turned war-torn Belgrade, and family sacrifice into tennis immortality
text: Inspiring story of the day: âIt made us tougher, it made us more hungry for successâ - How Novak Djokovic turned war-torn Belgrade, and family sacrifice into tennis immortality Novak Djokovic âs path to tennis greatness began far away from the bright lights of Wimbledon, the Australian Open and the US Open. At 12, he was living through the 1999 NATO bombing of Belgrade, sleeping in a basement with his family while air-raid sirens sounded above them. At the same time, his parents, Srdjan and Dijana Djokovic, were struggling to find the money needed for his tennis career. Djokovic has often said those years changed him. The fear, long nights, lack of money and his parentsâ sacrifices gave him a strong reason to keep going and succeed. How did Novak Djokovic keep playing tennis during the 1999 Belgrade bombings In 1999, Novak Djokovic was still a child, but his life was already very different from that of most young tennis players. NATO carried out an air campaign against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that lasted 78 days. Djokovic and his family spent nights in the basement of his grandfather Vladimirâs apartment building in Belgrade. The family apartment was small, and many relatives stayed there because there was nowhere else to go. When the sirens began, everyone moved downstairs for safety. Djokovic later told CBS News that the bombing made it difficult to stay focused, but he still continued playing tennis. âItâs the fear of the unknown. Not knowing if the next bomb is going to hit your headâ¦ We were waking up every single night more or less at two, three a.m. for two and a half months. But it made us tougher. It made us more hungry, more hungry for the success.â The tennis did not stop simply because the city was under attack. Djokovic and his coach Jelena Gencic looked for places where he could train. BBC Sport reported that he trained at different clubs around Belgrade, including Partizan Tennis Club, while people in the city helped him continue practicing. For Djokovic, tennis became something he could still control when almost everything around him felt uncertain. The experience did not make the bombing less frightening, but it gave him a reason to keep moving forward. What did Novak Djokovicâs family do to keep his tennis dream alive The war was only one part of the struggle. Money was another major problem. Djokovicâs parents ran a small pizza and pancake business in the Kopaonik mountains. Supporting a young tennis player was expensive, especially in a country facing serious economic problems. His family had to find money for coaching, equipment, travel and other costs linked to his development. Djokovic has spoken about going out early in the morning with his grandfather to find bread for the family. He remembered how many relatives were living together in a small apartment during those difficult years. âI remember standing in line with my grandfather at 5 in the morning to get bread to feed our whole familyâmy grandfather, my aunt, my uncle, my cousins, my siblings, my parents and I. We all lived together in a small apartment because we had no other choice, and those are the things that became an integral part of my character, of who I am today as a person.â His family also took major financial risks for his tennis. Reports about Djokovicâs childhood have described his father taking loans at high interest to help pay for his development. The family was sometimes left with almost nothing after covering the costs of his training. That struggle became an important part of how Djokovic viewed his career. Tennis was no longer just a sport he enjoyed. His parents were putting their own lives under pressure so that he could chase a future they believed was possible. Why did Novak Djokovic feel responsible for his parentsâ sacrifices Djokovic has never separated his success from what his parents went through for him. He has repeatedly spoken about the importance of family and the pressure he felt to make their sacrifices count. He once explained that his family background gave him a strong sense of responsibility: âSerbian history tells that family is the most important thing and you have to stick with the family. My parents went through a lot of hardships, financially, emotionally, every wayâ¦ To see my parents struggle so much just so I could play tennis, it gave me a responsibility and a drive that never left me.â That feeling stayed with him even after he became one of the biggest names in tennis. The Djokovic family had not started with the money or facilities available to many players at the top level. Novak had to leave Serbia as a young teenager to train at the Niki Pilic Tennis Academy in Germany, another major step in a career that demanded sacrifices from the whole family. The story is also important because Djokovicâs success did not come overnight. He had already spent years dealing with uncertainty before he began winning major titles. By the time he became a Grand Slam champion, he had learned to keep working even when conditions were far from ideal. How did Novak Djokovicâs childhood shape the champion he became Today, Djokovicâs records are huge. He has won 24 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record 10 Australian Open crowns, and he won Olympic singles gold at the Paris 2024 Games. He also holds the record for most weeks at world No. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines 1, with 428 weeks. The 2026 US Open ended with a first-round loss to Mariano Navone, but none of those later results changes the story of how his career began. The mental strength seen in Djokovicâs biggest matches can be understood better when his childhood is put into context. He learned very early that fear does not always mean you stop. Sometimes, you still have to wake up, find food, go to practice and keep working. His own words explain what those years meant to him: Novak Djokovic conquered tennis history through sheer willpower, discipline, and grit, but his mental armor was forged in the fire of his childhood. By honoring the sacrifices of his parents and never forgetting where he came from, he proves that true champions are built not in comfort, but through the courage to rise above adversity and fight for the people who believed in you. The quote captures the bigger part of Djokovicâs story. The trophies came much later. title: 8 Semi-Finals, 11 Slams, No 25th Yet: Can Novak Djokovic finally end his Grand Slam drought at US Open 2026?
text: Novak Djokovic during a practice session at the US Open in New York. (AP Photo) Three years after winning his historic 24th Grand Slam title, Novak Djokovic returns to New York still chasing the elusive 25th. At 39, the Serbian legend remains capable of competing with the best â but with time running out, can the stars finally align at Flushing Meadows? The last time Djokovic stood on Arthur Ashe Stadium for a Grand Slam final, he was making history. On September 10, 2023, Djokovic defeated Daniil Medvedev to win the US Open and claim his 24th Grand Slam singles title, drawing level with Margaret Court's all-time record. Almost three years later, that number remains unchanged. The 2026 US Open, therefore, is about more than another major. It is another attempt to break a record that has stubbornly remained just out of reach. Yet calling the period since his 2023 triumph a slump would be misleading. Djokovic has continued to reach the latter stages of Grand Slams with remarkable consistency. He has reached the semi-finals or better in eight of the last 11 majors, including two finals. What he has been unable to do is win one. Djokovic keeps getting close â but No. 25 remains elusive The Serbian's Grand Slam record since his 2023 US Open triumph tells the story. The numbers underline an intriguing contradiction. Djokovic has been a semi-finalist or better in eight of 11 Slams but has failed to add a single title to his collection. His two final appearances came at Wimbledon in 2024 and the Australian Open in 2026, while his latest deep run ended in the Wimbledon 2026 semi-finals against Jannik Sinner. This is not a case of a 39-year-old suddenly becoming incapable of competing with the best. Rather, Djokovic has remained good enough to get within touching distance of another major â but not quite good enough to take the final step. And that distinction could be crucial in New York. The longest wait for a Slam since his first title? If Djokovic fails again at the 2026 US Open, his wait for a Grand Slam title will stretch to 12 consecutive majors. That would be extraordinary for a player who has dominated men's tennis for so long. After winning his first major at the 2008 Australian Open, Djokovic endured an 11-Slam wait before claiming his second at the 2011 Australian Open. He was 23 when he finally ended that drought. A later slump saw him go eight Slams without a title before he ended that wait by winning Wimbledon in 2018. From his 13th major, however, Djokovic needed only six years to reach 24. That makes his current drought historically significant. For the first time since the early years of his career, Djokovic is facing the possibility of going three full years without winning a Grand Slam. The difference now, of course, is age. He was 23 when he ended his first major drought. He is 39 now. Alcaraz and Sinner have changed everything Age is only part of the explanation for Djokovic's inability to turn deep runs into another title. The bigger factor has been the emergence of Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner. Since Djokovic won his 24th major in New York in 2023, Alcaraz and Sinner have won 10 of the last 11 Grand Slam titles, with Alexander Zverev taking the 2026 French Open. That is perhaps the most telling statistic in Djokovic's pursuit. He has not been pushed out of the elite. He has simply encountered a new generation that has become exceptionally difficult to beat when the stakes are highest. Alcaraz has beaten Djokovic three times in Grand Slam finals, while Sinner has emerged as another major obstacle. Yet Djokovic's head-to-head records show why he cannot simply be written off. He is 5-5 against Alcaraz and trails Sinner only 5-6. That is remarkable for a player approaching 40. The difference is that the younger pair have been more effective at converting their opportunities into Grand Slam trophies. The 2026 US Open could finally give Djokovic an opening This is what makes the 2026 US Open particularly intriguing. The draw has presented Djokovic with circumstances that have been missing from several of his recent Grand Slam attempts. Most importantly, Sinner is absent after withdrawing with a knee injury. Alcaraz, meanwhile, is returning after a lengthy layoff caused by a wrist injury, leaving questions over whether he can immediately reproduce his best Grand Slam tennis. Djokovic has also avoided 2026 French Open champion Zverev until a potential final. His projected route is difficult but manageable, with a potential quarter-final against Medvedev and Alcaraz among the biggest threats in the latter stages. Compared with recent Slams, Djokovic has one major advantage: one of his two biggest young rivals is absent and the other is returning from injury. The stars, at least on paper, appear to be aligning. Novak Djokovic (AP Photo) But Djokovic's biggest opponent may be time There is one factor no draw can remove: age. Djokovic's physical resilience has been one of the defining features of his career. Even at 39, he continues to produce performances that would be extraordinary for almost any other player. His Olympic gold medal in Paris in 2024 was proof that he could still summon his best tennis for a massive occasion. But his overall record since 2023 also reflects the realities of getting older. He won only one title in 2024 and two in 2025, while he remains without a title in 2026 before the US Open. His last ATP Finals appearance also came in 2023, and injuries have increasingly affected his schedule. Preparation has therefore become another question mark. Djokovic does not need to dominate the season anymore. He needs to produce two perfect weeks. At 39, that is considerably harder. Can Djokovic finally win No. 25? The answer is yes â but perhaps never has a Djokovic Grand Slam campaign carried so many qualifications. He is still good enough. The numbers prove it. Eight semi-finals or better in his last 11 Slams demonstrate that he remains capable of navigating the toughest tournaments in tennis. Two of those runs ended in finals. But he is no longer the overwhelming favourite he once was. Alcaraz and Sinner have won 10 of the last 11 majors. Djokovic has repeatedly been stopped at the final hurdle or just before it. And at 39, every Grand Slam represents a diminishing opportunity to add to a record that already borders on untouchable. The 2026 US Open, however, may be different. Sinner is absent. Alcaraz is returning from injury. Zverev is in the other half. Djokovic has four US Open titles and 10 finals in New York, giving him a level of experience few in the field can match. Most importantly, he still believes. The question is whether he can win the two matches that have eluded him for almost three years â and finally turn 24 into 25. At 39, it could be his last great chance. title: Lausanne Diamond League: Why Neeraj Chopra has more at stake today than settling score with Pathirage
text: Rumesh Pathirage and Neeraj Chopra (PTI Photo) Neeraj Chopra will meet Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage for the third time this season when the two javelin stars return to the Diamond League stage in Lausanne on Friday night. The rivalry has so far been one-sided. Pathirage has beaten Chopra in both of their meetings this season, first in Doha and then at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where the Sri Lankan produced a 89.75m throw for gold and Chopra settled for silver with a season-best 85.83m. For Chopra, however, Lausanne is about more than changing that head-to-head record. He is also trying to strengthen his position in the Diamond League standings, with his place in the season-ending final not yet secured. Pathirage has been the man to beat Pathirage arrives in Lausanne having produced the best season of his young career. The 23-year-old has won eight of the nine competitions he has entered this season, including Diamond League victories in Doha and Rome and the Commonwealth Games title in Glasgow. He also owns the 2026 world-leading throw of 92.62m, recorded at the Golden Gala in Rome in June. That came after his 88.68m winning throw in Doha, where he finished ahead of Chopra, who managed 85.69m for fourth place. Glasgow: Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage makes an attempt during the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026, in Glasgow, Scotland. Pathirage wins the gold medal in this event. (PTI Photo/Ravi Choudhary)(PTI08_01_2026_000159B) Their second meeting came in Glasgow last month. Pathirage again took gold, this time with 89.75m, while Chopra improved on his Doha performance with 85.83m. That leaves Pathirage with a 2-0 advantage over Chopra this season, and the distance between their best throws is currently significant. Chopra returns to a venue where he has excelled Lausanne is nevertheless a familiar and successful venue for Chopra. He won the meeting in 2022 with 89.08m and returned the following year to win again with 87.66m. In 2024, he finished second after throwing 89.49m. His Diamond League breakthrough came in 2022, although his involvement in the series dates back to 2017, when he competed in Paris, Monaco and Zurich. Glasgow: India's Neeraj Chopra during the men's javelin throw final at the Commonwealth Games 2026, in Glasgow, Scotland. Chopra wins the silver medal in this event. (PTI Photo/Ravi Choudhary)(PTI08_01_2026_000161A) Chopra's Diamond League personal best remains the 90.23m he threw in Doha in 2025, while he also won the Paris meeting that year. His only Diamond League appearance so far in 2026 came in Doha, where his 85.69m was enough for fourth place. The Tokyo 2020 Olympic champion now arrives in Lausanne after his silver-medal performance in Glasgow, where his 85.83m remains his season best. Why Lausanne matters for Chopra's Diamond League qualification The Lausanne competition carries particular importance because Chopra has not yet officially qualified for the 2026 Diamond League Final. He currently sits seventh in the standings with six points, while only the top six in the javelin standings automatically qualify for the final, which will be held in Brussels on September 4 and 5. Pathirage and Anderson Peters have already secured their places after collecting 23 and 22 points respectively. That makes every available point important for Chopra. After Lausanne, there is only one more Diamond League meeting featuring the men's javelin, Zurich on August 27, giving him limited opportunities to improve his position before the final qualification picture is settled. Chopra has previously won the Diamond League Final in 2022 and finished runner-up in 2023, 2024 and 2025. A strong field awaits Pathirage may have the momentum, but Chopra will have plenty of competition beyond his Sri Lankan rival. Two-time Olympic medallist Keshorn Walcott, the reigning world champion Anderson Peters and Czech veteran Jakub Vadlejch are all in the field. title: What happened between Simone Biles and the influencer she suddenly unfollowed? 11-time Olympic medalist reveals
text: Simone Biles (Getty Images) Simone Biles does not tolerate pettiness -- not even from someone she genuinely admired. The 11-time Olympic medalist went on TikTok this week and shared a story that has apparently stayed with her for years. It involves an influencer she followed for a long time, a simple request for a hairstylist's contact, and a response so oddly guarded that Biles decided the follow was not worth keeping. Why did Simone Biles unfollow the influencer she had been following for years? Simone Biles had been following this particular influencer for years, genuinely inspired by her aesthetic. As she put it, "her style, her content, she was super super cute, but her hair was always slayed to a T." So when she wanted a referral, it felt like a natural thing to ask. Biles, a four-time Olympic gold medalist, reached out asking for the influencer's hairstylist's booking information -- and that is when things got strange. The influencer replied: "Bless. My manager has it. I'll have to ask her." Biles was baffled. "What? You don't know who does your hair appointments? You don't have their contact or Instagram?" What makes this even more telling is the context Biles added around it. "I get gatekeeping, but to a certain extent," she said. "Mind you, we lived in two different states, so I think maybe she thought I was going to steal her hairstylist or something. But that's not at all what it was, like I travel all the time -- so if I'm ever in that area, let me get slay." There is something quietly sharp about that line. Biles is one of the most recognizable athletes in the world. She was not looking to poach anyone. She just wanted a good stylist recommendation while on the road. The paranoia behind the influencer's response -- treating a friendly inquiry like a competitive threat -- apparently said everything Biles needed to know about the dynamic. After the interaction left her feeling off, Biles made the call to unfollow, saying plainly, "I didn't need that kind of negativity in my life." It is a short story, but it lands. Biles did not name the influencer, and she was not particularly bitter about it either. She told the story the way you would tell a friend -- with a slight shake of the head and a shrug that says, "some people just aren't worth it." That kind of composed self-awareness, especially from someone who has faced far heavier public scrutiny than most, feels very on-brand for her. title: After Jaspal Ranaâs sudden demise, Paris Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker forging new bonds with Serbian coach
text: Manu Bhaker with her new coach (Photo by Jelena Arunovic) BHOPAL: After adjusting the lighting at the MP State Shooting Academy final hall, two young electricians asked Manu Bhaker if she needed anything else. âNahin,â the shooting star politely replied. With that stardom and popularity that surrounds her, the Paris Olympics double medallist may have realised at that moment, that a lot rides on her validation. She has a different weapon now -- flexibility. While a certain doggedness suited her teenage self, flexibility is becoming of a mature Manu. Other than being a good judge of situations, Manu is also mastering the art of changing according to its demands. After the sudden passing away of her coach, Jaspal Rana, two months back, Manu has adapted herself with Serbian coach Jelena Arunovic. title: Who is Georgia Hunter Bell? Meet the sprinter chasing a stunning âGrand Slamâ in September 2026 following heroics in European Athletics Championships
text: Georgia Hunter Bell(via Getty) Georgia Hunter Bell is enjoying one of the best seasons of her athletics career. The 32-year-old Great Britain star won the womenâs 1500m gold at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham on Sunday. She clocked 4:07.78 and finished more than a second ahead of Polandâs Klaudia Kazimierska. The victory is another major achievement in an extraordinary comeback story. Hunter Bell walked away from athletics for five years before returning to the sport. She has now won the 1500m at the World Indoor Championships and the 800m at the Commonwealth Games in 2026. Her latest European title has put her on course for a possible fourth major title later this year. Who is Georgia Hunter Bell? Inside her early life, family and remarkable athletics comeback Georgia Hunter Bell was born Georgia Bell on October 17, 1993, in Paris, France. She grew up in London and showed her talent for athletics from a young age. Bell was already a highly rated middle-distance runner as a teenager. She won the English Schools under-15 800m title. At just 14, she ran 2:08.81 for the distance. That performance placed her among the leading young runners in Britain. Her family also has strong links to journalism and education. Her father, Andy Bell, is a political journalist. Her mother, Angela Bell, is a school PE teacher. Georgia has two sisters. She later married George Hunter in October 2024. Bell attended Cardinal Vaughan Memorial School before studying geography at the University of Birmingham. She later moved to the United States to study at the University of California, Berkeley, where she continued her athletics career. However, her first chapter in elite athletics did not end the way she had hoped. Injuries and the pressures of the American collegiate system affected her progress. She eventually stepped away from athletics at the age of 23. Bell spent around five years away from competitive running. During that period, she worked in technology sales. Her career included working for a London-based company involved in cybersecurity. Her return to athletics began almost by accident. During the pandemic period, Bell took part in a local Parkrun. She quickly discovered that her speed was still there. How Parkrun helped Georgia Hunter Bellâs comeback The Parkrun became the starting point for one of athleticsâ most remarkable comebacks. Bell reconnected with former coaches Trevor Painter and Jenny Meadows and returned to serious training. She also joined Belgrave Harriers. Her improvement was rapid. In 2024, she made the Great Britain team for the Paris Olympics. She went on to win bronze in the 1500m final and set a British record of 3:52.61. She also won silver at the 2024 European Championships. Her 2026 season has taken her career to another level. Bell won the World Indoor 1500m title in Torun in March, setting a British indoor record of 3:58.53. She then won Commonwealth Games gold in the 800m in Glasgow. title: Who is Meghan Musnicki? Meet two-time American Olympic gold medalist who has found a new challenge after rowing retirement
text: Regina Salmons, Madeline Wanamaker and Meghan Musnicki try on clothes at the Team USA Welcome Experience Ahead of Paris 2024 (via Getty) Meghan Musnicki has started a new chapter after retiring from rowing following the Paris 2024 Olympics. The two-time Olympic gold medalist is now working in preventive health and preparing for a completely different sporting challenge, her first marathon. Musnicki competed at four Summer Olympics and won gold in the womenâs eight at London 2012 and Rio 2016. At 41, she became the oldest American woman to compete in Olympic rowing when she represented the United States at Paris 2024. After retiring, she joined preventive health company Biograph and discovered important information about her own cardiovascular health. Who is Meghan Musnicki? Inside her career and Olympics rowing journey Meghan Musnickiâs journey into rowing began unexpectedly during her freshman year at St. Lawrence University in 2001. She had gone to the athletic department hoping to try out for basketball. Instead, a rowing coach encouraged her to try the sport, even though she had little idea about rowing at the time. She later transferred to Ithaca College and became an important member of its rowing programme. She helped the college win NCAA Division III titles in 2004 and 2005. After graduating in 2005 with a Bachelor of Science in Psychology, she continued pursuing rowing and attended U.S. national team selection camps. Her breakthrough came in 2010 when she made the U.S. national team. She also won her first World Rowing Championships gold medal that year in the womenâs eight. Two years later, Musnicki reached the biggest stage in sport. She helped the United States win Olympic gold in the womenâs eight at the London 2012 Games. She was part of the same successful boat at Rio 2016, securing a second consecutive Olympic title. She returned for Tokyo 2020, where the U.S. womenâs eight finished fourth. Musnicki then earned another Olympic selection for Paris 2024. The American crew did not win a medal, and Musnicki retired soon afterwards. Exploring Meghan Musnickiâs new career and health journey after Olympic rowing Meghan Musnickiâs post-rowing career took an unexpected turn when a friend introduced her to Biograph. She joined the company in membership development and partnerships. The role also gave her access to detailed health testing. Despite her elite athletic background, the testing revealed elevated LDL cholesterol, high Lp(a) and a genetic risk linked to cardiovascular disease. The discovery had a personal impact because her father died suddenly from a heart attack at 49. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Musnicki chose to treat the information as something useful rather than simply frightening. She worked with a dietitian and an exercise physiologist and made lifestyle changes. She said her Lp(a) fell by roughly 25 to 30 points and her cholesterol dropped by about 30 points within six months. Her approach to training has also changed. She now prioritises heavy strength training, Zone 2 cardio, sprint sessions, jumping, plyometrics and mobility work to support muscle mass, bone density and long-term health. Musnicki is now taking on another challenge. She has bought a Garmin smartwatch and is training for her first marathon, marking a new sporting chapter after more than a decade at the highest level of rowing. title: Revanth Reddy not first CM to be denied MEA nod for foreign visit
text: Revanth Reddy joins list of opposition leaders denied foreign travel clearance HYDERABAD: Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy is not the first CM to be denied political clearance by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to visit a foreign country for official purposes. Among the many opposition CMs and ministers from various states denied nod for a foreign tour, some had faced rejections multiple times. Sources, however, said Revanth is the first CM to be denied political clearance both after the formation of Telangana, and also in the united AP govt. According to various sources, Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann along with a 25-member delegation including state industries minister, was supposed to visit UK and Israel in February 2026 to attract investments, for which political clearance was rejected. Previously, the MEA had also declined clearance to Mann for his planned to visit Paris Olympics between Aug 3 to 9 in 2024 to support the Indian Hockey team. However, the Punjab CM was allowed to visit Japan and South Korea in Dec 2025. The Aam Aadmi Party had in Aug 2025 said that four of its Punjab ministers, including the CM, had been denied permission for foreign tours. The MEA had also turned down a request by Mamata Banerjee , the then CM of West Bengal, in September 2021, when she wanted to attend the World Peace Conference in Rome stating that the status of the event was not commensurate to the status of a CM. The Trinamool Congress chief and her party leaders had expressed their frustration on social media over the denial. Banerjee had also not got approval for her planned visit Chicago in 2018. In 2017, there were reports that she had been denied permission for a visit to China. However, the MEA had categorically denied that it had received any request from the then CM for the visit. Another opposition leader on the âdenialâ list is AAP chief Arvind Kejriwal . Back in Oct 2019, when Kejriwal was Delhi chief minister, he had been denied MEA nod for a visit to Denmark to attend the C40 climate summit. The MEA had reportedly stated that the event was meant for mayors of various cities not for CMs. Subsequently, he had also not got approval for his visit to Singapore in 2022. Kejriwalâs deputy CM Manish Sisodia was also denied permission in Nov 2018 to visit Austria. In Aug 2018, Sisodia had claimed his request to visit Moscow had been denied. The MEA had later approved his Russia visit. Another minister in Kejriwalâs govt, Satyaneder Jain was not allowed to visit Australia in Nov 2018. In Nov 2025, Pinarayi Vijayan , the then Kerala CM, did not get political clearance for a visit to Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Oman. He was supposed to hold official and diaspora meetings in these countries, which have large immigrant population from Kerala. This was the second time when he was not allowed to visit Gulf countries. In 2023, a meeting in Saudi Arabia was cancelled after he did not get clearance from MEA. During the UPA rule, the MEA had denied political clearance to a planned trip by Congress leader and then Assam CM Tarun Gogoi to the US for a high-level meeting in April 2012. He had also been denied permission to visit Israel. The then UPA govt had also denied Jharkhand CM Arjun Munda a nod to visit Thailand. What is political clearance? The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) grants to political clearnace. This is required to public servants and government servants for a foreign trip. The MEA takes decision whether to give political clearance or not based on multiple factors including the nature of the event, the kind of invitation, visiting country and its relations with India etc. What clearances do a chief ministers require to travel abroad? Many CMs of states visiting countries to attract investments. Chief Ministers are required to inform the Cabinet Secretariat as well as the MEA about any foreign visit, be it official or private. Prior political clearance and FCRA (Foreign Contribution Regulation Act) clearance is also mandatory. They also inform and get clearance from the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA). The DEA and the ministry concerned will entertain an application only if political clearance from the MEA is attached with the request. Without this clearance, no public servant can go abroad. title: What made Katie Ledecky different? Family support, relentless work ethic and the mindset behind Americaâs swimming legend
text: Katie Ledecky (Image Via Getty Images) Katie Ledecky âs evolution from teenage Olympic champion to one of the most decorated swimmers of all time has never been attributed to talent alone. The American distance specialist won her first Olympic gold in the 800m freestyle at London 2012 aged just 15 and proceeded to dominate the event through to Paris 2024. Now her career has spanned four Olympic Games and more than a decade at the top level of international swimming. USA Swimming, which lists her among the most decorated athletes in the sport, says her primary club is Gator Swim Club and her coach is Anthony Nesty. Whatâs interesting about Ledecky is that combination of being competitive and emotionally balanced. Her parents pushed her, but didnât turn swimming into a constant pressure, and Ledecky developed an unusually strong appetite for challenging training. She also developed a habit of setting personal âwant timesâ to measure her progress without focusing on opponents or medals. That mixture remains her modus operandi in 2026. Watch Katie Ledecky Answers Your Questions Katie Ledeckyâs mindset behind her swimming dominance in 2026 Ledeckyâs most unique psychological advantage is her ability to focus on what she can control. As a child, she would say âwant timesâ for ambitious performance goals. The clock was the main opponent, as she didn't focus her preparation on another swimmer. As her reputation grew, that approach became more valuable. Once Ledecky became the favorite in distance freestyle, winning alone wasnât as much of a developmental challenge. But still, there was a personal time, countable no matter who was in the next lane. Mindset factor Katie Ledeckyâs approach Main target Personal performance times Primary opponent The clock Focus during races Own execution and pace View of setbacks Opportunity to learn Long-term motivation Continuous improvement Ledecky has also developed a reputation for liking the hardest parts of swimming. Training is not simply a necessary rite of passage before competition; it is one of the areas in which she measures progress. Another important component of her approach is a readiness to accept imperfect play. Fear of failure can trap elite athletes when past success creates expectations that are impossible to meet. Ledeckyâs approach is different because training gives a controlled environment to test those limits. Katie Ledeckyâs family support shaped her fearless approach Another big part of Ledeckyâs development was the family atmosphere around her. Her parents, David and Mary Gen Ledecky, provided the emotional and logistical support needed of an elite athlete, while leaving swimming-specific instruction to professional coaches. Family influence Impact on Ledecky Emotional support Reduced performance-related pressure Older brother Michael Early exposure to competitive swimming Parental involvement Practical support without controlling coaching Education Broader identity beyond sport Family stability Greater freedom to pursue ambitious goals That separation counts. When a young athlete starts to produce exceptional results, itâs easy for parents to get over-involved. For Ledecky, the family environment meant that swimming was something she did because she enjoyed it, not because she needed to get approval. Ledeckyâs family also played a big role in her beginning competitive swimming. Katie had an early example to follow in the household, with her older brother, Michael Ledecky, already in the pool. It wasn't simply influence vs. competition. Training can seem daunting, but if you have a sibling who does the same activity, it can seem more familiar and fun. It also set an early competitive benchmark that helped Ledecky get comfortable trying herself out. Education also mattered a great deal to the Ledecky family. That helped establish an identity for Katie that was more than just swimming. Katie Ledeckyâs training habits sustain her historic success Ledeckyâs success is based on an incredible combination of endurance, pacing and technique. In distance freestyle, swimmers have to pace themselves and conserve energy over hundreds or even thousands of meters. Her technique, therefore, has been a constant work of refinement. Stroke efficiency, kicking, breathing patterns, turns, and pacing can all mean the difference between an excellent world-class performance and a historically fast one. Her place at the top of distance swimming extended to 2026. Ledecky is still turning in elite times, competing for Gator Swim Clu, USA Swimming records. Westmont, 2026 TYR Pro Swim Series: Won the womenâs 800-meter freestyle in 8:08.57. Ledecky remains the American and world record-holder in the 1,500-meter freestyle, according to USA Swimmingâs 2026 records. Her 15:20.48 mark from 2018 has yet to be broken. Career achievement Katie Ledecky Olympic Games competed 4 through Paris 2024 First Olympic appearance London 2012 Olympic gold medals through Paris 2024 9 Olympic medals through Paris 2024 14 Primary events 800m and 1,500m freestyle Current club Gator Swim Club 1,500m freestyle world record 15:20.48 What is remarkable about Ledeckyâs career is not just the sheer number of championships. Itâs the length of time she has remained capable of producing performances that would be career-defining achievements for most swimmers. She built on that legacy with another haul of medals at Paris 2024. Her Olympic resume now stretches from a breakthrough in London as a teenager to success more than a decade later. Katie Ledeckyâs legacy goes beyond medals By 2026, Ledeckyâs legacy is increasingly about the way she goes about pursuing greatness as much as the records sheâs racked up. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines Her family was a stable support without making medals a prerequisite for approval. Her training philosophy turned tough workouts into opportunities for growth. Her âwant timesâ were like an internal yardstick. But most importantly, her mindset kept her focused on the controllables as the swimming world started measuring itself against her. Ledeckyâs size and speed are why sheâs still such a force in American swimming. The medals are the visible evidence, but the deeper story is the system behind them: support without pressure, ambition without obsession with rivals, and a willingness to go back to the pool every day looking for another improvement. title: 17 years on, from Hyderabad to New Delhi: How India became a badminton powerhouse
text: Satwiksairaj Rankireddy, Chirag Shetty, and PV Sindhu When the worldâs best badminton players walk into the Indira Gandhi Indoor Stadium on Monday, India will not merely be hosting the World Championships for the second time. Seventeen years after Hyderabad staged the event, the tournament returns to a country where badminton has grown multiple folds â in popularity, participation, elite success and commercial reach. The transformation is visible in the numbers. Forty-three per cent of Indians follow badminton, while 32% actively participate in the sport, making it the country's second-most played sport and its leading racket sport. At the Paris Olympics, badminton was the most-followed sport among Indian consumers, with 21% saying they would follow it, according to a YouGov poll. In 2009, India was already a passionate badminton nation, but the sport's footprint today is on an entirely different scale. Watch Indiaâs big home advantage at BWF World Championships: Pressure & medal hopes From a host to a major badminton market India now hosts four BWF World Tour tournaments every year, underlining its importance on the international calendar. The India Open alone reached a potential 403 million household viewers across broadcast and digital platforms in 2024. That commercial growth has been accompanied by a much deeper Indian presence at the highest level. India's first World Championships medal came through Prakash Padukone in 1983. Since 2011, however, an Indian player or pair has won a medal at every edition, creating a remarkable 15-year streak of podium finishes. From Padukone to Sindhu, Satwik-Chirag The list of medallists also shows how India's strength has expanded across generations and disciplines. Saina Nehwal won silver in 2015 and bronze in 2017, while PV Sindhu became India's biggest World Championships star, winning five medals, including the country's first and only gold in 2019. Kidambi Srikanth won silver and Lakshya Sen bronze in 2021, HS Prannoy added another men's singles bronze in 2023, while Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty have established India as a force in men's doubles with medals in 2022 and 2025. The three Olympic medals won by Indian badminton players â Saina's bronze at London 2012 and Sindhu's silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020 â further underline the country's rise. And perhaps the biggest sign of the sport's expanding ecosystem is para-badminton. India now has more than 1,000 athletes in national training programmes and 302 internationally classified players, while Indian para-badminton athletes have won more than 1,200 international medals in the past decade. The country has also collected nine Paralympic badminton medals, including golds at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. A very different India from Hyderabad 2009 The contrast with the last World Championships in India is striking. Hyderabad 2009 was dominated by China, which won four of the five gold medals. Three of the five finals featured players or pairs from the same country, reflecting the concentration of power that characterised the sport at the time. The badminton world has since become considerably more competitive â and India has been an important part of that transformation. Countries such as Japan, Chinese Taipei, Thailand and India have established themselves as regular contenders, while France, Canada and Singapore have also produced major breakthroughs. World champions have emerged from nations that once had little presence at the very top, including Thailand, Spain, Singapore and Malaysia. India, meanwhile, has gone from being represented by individual stars to becoming a multi-discipline medal contender. Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines New Delhi represents the next chapter That makes the return of the World Championships to India more than a 17-year homecoming. It is a reflection of how far the sport has travelled in the country since Hyderabad. The numbers tell the story: a massive participation base, a huge fan following, four annual World Tour events, a rapidly expanding commercial footprint and an Indian medal at every World Championships since 2011. There is also a new generation ready to carry that legacy forward. If Hyderabad 2009 showcased India as an enthusiastic host watching the world's best, New Delhi 2026 arrives with India firmly established as one of badminton's major global markets and competitive forces. Seventeen years ago, India hosted the World Championships. This time, it hosts them as a badminton powerhouse â and with the opportunity to add another chapter to a remarkable rise. title: 8-0 becomes 8-1: 'Impatient' PV Sindhu falls to cramping Wang Zhi Yi in epic duel
text: PV Sindhu in action on Day 4 of the BWF World Championships. (BAI) NEW DELHI: Up until the start of 2024, PV Sindhu had never lost to a Chinese shuttler at the Olympics and the BWF World Championships . An unblemished 9-0 record. I don't know if she was injured or not. That was maybe her strategy of doing it. You never know. Maybe that's her gameplay. I'm aware that players engage in such tactics, but I was really injured Wang Zhi Yi "I can understand that in that moment it looked like she had such a thought but I was really injured. I'm aware that players engage in such tactics, but I was really injured," claimed the three-time World Junior Championships medallist. The ensuing points, from 16-15 in the third game, Sindhu believes, turned the match. While the 31-year-old Indian started to get impatient, by her own admission, the Chinese shuttler fought on. PV Sindhu, who will now shift her focus to the Asian Games, took a philosophical approach to her exit. "Disappointed of course. That's how sport is. You learn, you lose a lot, you win a lot. title: CWG 2026 stars join IOS Sports family as agency expands elite athlete roster
text: IOS Sports & Entertainment has expanded its elite athlete roster with the signing of seven accomplished Indian athletes, including six Commonwealth Games 2026 medallists, strengthening the agency's presence across boxing, judo and para-athletics. The new additions are boxers Priya Ghanghas, Arundhati Choudhary, Jadumani Singh Mandengbam and Ankush Panghal, judoka Asmita Dey, para-athlete Sharmila Dhankar and para-javelin thrower Navdeep Singh. The signings add further depth to an IOS portfolio that already features several of India's leading Olympic, Paralympic and non-cricket sporting personalities. The latest group collectively secured six medals at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Priya Ghanghas, Arundhati Choudhary, Asmita Dey, Sharmila Dhankar and Ankush Panghal won gold, while Jadumani Singh claimed silver. Glasgow success brings new faces into IOS fold Priya Ghanghas has quickly established herself as one of India's promising young boxers. The 20-year-old won the women's 60kg gold medal at the Commonwealth Games, defeating Canada's Marie-Bathoul Al-Ahmadieh in the final. Her Glasgow triumph came after another major success earlier in the year, when she won gold at the Asian Boxing Championships in Ulaanbaatar. Arundhati Choudhary also enjoyed a breakthrough year, winning the women's 70kg gold at the Commonwealth Games. The Rajasthan boxer had already made her mark on the senior international circuit with gold at the 2025 World Boxing Cup Finals after returning from injury. Her Commonwealth Games victory further strengthened her position among India's leading women boxers. Jadumani Singh Mandengbam marked his Commonwealth Games debut with a silver medal in the men's 55kg category. The Manipuri boxer had reached the semifinals of the 2025 World Boxing Cup in Brazil and secured his place in the Glasgow squad after an impressive showing at the national trials. Ankush Panghal, another Commonwealth Games debutant, won gold in the men's 80kg boxing category. The 22-year-old produced a memorable comeback in the final against England's Dimeji Shittu, recovering from a difficult opening round to secure a 4-1 victory and claim the title. Historic milestones across judo and para-sport Asmita Dey added another historic achievement to the group. She became the first Indian judoka to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal, triumphing in the women's 48kg category in Glasgow. Dey defeated Canada's Heidi Quach in a dramatic Golden Score final. Her international record also includes gold at the 2025 Casablanca African Open and a fifth-place finish at the 2026 Asian Senior Championships. Para-athlete Sharmila Dhankar also created history at Glasgow 2026 by winning gold in the women's F57 shot put with a season-best throw of 9.81m. Her victory ended India's 20-year wait for a Commonwealth Games medal in para-athletics and made her the country's first Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the discipline. Navdeep Singh brings significant international experience to the IOS roster. The F41 javelin thrower is the reigning Paralympic champion after winning gold at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games. He has continued to compete on the World Para Athletics circuit in 2026 as he builds towards upcoming major international competitions. Building careers beyond medals Rahul Trehan, Chief Operating Officer, IOS Sports & Entertainment, said, âWe are delighted to welcome Priya, Arundhati, Asmita, Jadumani, Ankush, Sharmila and Navdeep to the IOS family. What makes them special is not just their medals, but the resilience and determination behind them. From overcoming injuries to breaking new ground in para-sport and rising to the very top of their disciplines, each athlete has a story of perseverance. The agency's existing athlete portfolio includes Vijender Singh, Anju Bobby George, Mirabai Chanu, Lovlina Borgohain, Manpreet Singh, Manika Batra, Hardik Singh, Sumit Antil, Nishad Kumar and Nitesh Kumar, among others. title: USA Basketball makes long awaited Caitlin Clark decision as Womenâs World Cup roster finally settles Olympic debate
text: USA Basketball makes long awaited Caitlin Clark decision as Womenâs World Cup roster finally settles Olympic debate Caitlin Clark has officially earned her place on the USA Womenâs World Cup team, ending months of questions about whether she would return to the national squad after missing the Paris Olympics in 2024. USA Basketball announced its 12-player roster on Thursday for next monthâs FIBA Womenâs World Cup in Germany, with Clark included after a standout stretch for the Indiana Fever. Her selection comes two years after one of the biggest talking points in womenâs basketball, when she was left off the Olympic team despite entering the WNBA as one of the sportâs biggest stars. Caitlin Clark earns USA Womenâs World Cup spot after missing Paris Olympics Caitlin Clarkâs selection closes the chapter on one of the most debated decisions in recent USA Basketball history. In 2024, she was not included in the roster for the Paris Olympics, even though she had become one of the biggest names in basketball following her record-breaking college career and her arrival in the WNBA. At the time, USA Basketball explained that the final roster was built around experience and team chemistry. The decision drew strong reactions from fans, players, and analysts, with many believing Clark had done enough to deserve a place on the team. Despite the criticism, the United States went on to win its eighth straight Olympic gold medal. Now, Clark has secured her place for the World Cup after continuing to prove herself at the professional level. USA Basketball confirmed her selection on Thursday as part of the 12-player squad that will represent the United States in Germany next month. The Indiana Fever guard has continued to grow into one of the biggest faces of womenâs basketball since being selected with the No. 1 overall pick in the 2024 WNBA Draft. Before turning professional, she finished her college career at Iowa as the highest scorer in NCAA Division I basketball history, breaking records that had stood for years. Caitlin Clarkâs record-breaking WNBA form helped seal World Cup selection Clarkâs recent performances played a major role in strengthening her case for the national team. During a remarkable July, she became the first player in WNBA history to record at least 40 points and 10 assists in a single game, adding another milestone to her growing list of achievements. She also scored 45 points in a game, setting a new Indiana Fever franchise record. Those performances came during one of the best stretches of her young professional career and showed why she remains one of the leagueâs most exciting players. title: "He was begging me to play with him": Who slid into whose DMs? Aryna Sabalenka reveals the truth about her US Open team-up with Novak Djokovic
text: Novak Djokovic ,Aryna Sabalenka (Getty Images) Fresh off a convincing win over Talia Gibson at the Cincinnati Open, Aryna Sabalenka had barely left the court when the questions shifted from her serve to her social life. Specifically: did Novak Djokovic slide into her DMs to recruit her for the US Open mixed doubles? Sabalenka played it cool for about two seconds before letting it all out. Yes, they are teaming up at Flushing Meadows. Yes, Djokovic asked first. And yes, the world No. 1 had some fun at the 24-time Grand Slam champion's expense while confirming the whole thing. Did Novak Djokovic ask Aryna Sabalenka to play mixed doubles at the US Open 2026 ? Yes, and Aryna Sabalenka made sure everyone knew who made the first move. When the reporter teasingly asked who slid into whose DMs, she did not hesitate. "Well you know, he was begging me to play with him. I said 'you know what... Of course legend, I'll help you out. Let's try to have fun and go for the title.' So I guess it's true. We are playing. It's gonna be so much fun. I'm super excited," she said, laughing. The exchange was exactly the kind of candid moment that reminds you why Sabalenka is one of the most entertaining figures in tennis right now. Not just a force on the court, but someone who says what she actually thinks. And what she thinks is that she did Djokovic a favour. The legend needed her help. She obliged. For context, this is not the first time these two have shared a court. They played together at the 2024 Australian Open charity event, a sold-out night at Rod Laver Arena that gave fans a preview of what this pairing looks like in motion. The chemistry was obvious even then. Now they have a proper competition to chase. When and where will Sabalenka and Djokovic play mixed doubles at the US Open? The 2026 US Open Mixed Doubles Championship runs from August 24 to 26, with matches across Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium. A new eight-team qualifying tournament is set for August 24, followed by the main draw on August 25 and 26. The event was revamped in 2025 with a $1 million prize for the winning pair, a move designed to pull in top singles players rather than doubles specialists. It worked. Sabalenka and Djokovic headline a genuinely star-studded entry list. Iga Swiatek and Casper Ruud return as 2025 runners-up. Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori come in as defending champions. Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz are in the draw. So are Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper, and in a fascinating debut, Filipina star Alexandra Eala partnering with Felix Auger-Aliassime. Djokovic has prior experience in this format at Flushing Meadows. Last year he paired with compatriot Olga Danilovic, but they fell in the opening round against Mirra Andreeva and Daniil Medvedev. The 39-year-old will be looking for a much better run this time, with arguably a far stronger partner beside him. Are Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic serious about winning the US Open mixed doubles title? The banter may be loud, but the intent is clear. Sabalenka left no room for doubt on that front. "Mixed doubles, I played it once in my life, I mean on the Grand Slams, and we are going full, you know, we're chasing only the title, that's our goal, I believe, so it's going to be fun and intense," she said at the Canadian Open press conference. That is the thing about this pairing that makes it genuinely interesting. Neither of them is turning up for the experience. Sabalenka holds the world No. 1 ranking and has two US Open singles titles to her name. Djokovic has 24 Grand Slam titles and a Paris 2024 Olympic gold medal. When two people wired like that say they are going for the title, you believe them. Sabalenka is also coming into this North American hard-court swing with something to prove. She has maintained her No. 1 ranking through 2026 but has not won a Grand Slam singles title this season, falling short in Melbourne, Paris, and London. Whether that translates on court is another question entirely. But if Sabalenka's Cincinnati press conference is any indicator, they will at least be the most fun to watch. title: Can Keely Hodgkinson become the first British woman to achieve European 800m hat-trick in European Athletics Championships following Olympics glory?
text: Keely Hodgkinson (via Getty) Keely Hodgkinson is aiming to make history at the European Athletics Championships in Birmingham. The British Olympic champion is chasing a third consecutive European 800m gold medal. If she succeeds, she would become the first British woman to win the same individual event three times at the European Championships. Hodgkinson has already won European titles in 2022 and 2024. Now, she faces a strong challenge from Swiss star Audrey Werro and Dutch athlete Femke Bol . Despite her Olympic success, Hodgkinson insists the chance to win gold in front of a home crowd would be just as special as her triumph in Paris. Keely Hodgkinson eyes historic third European title ahead of European Athletics Championships in Birmingham The womenâs 800m is expected to be one of the biggest races of the championships. Keely Hodgkinson enters the competition as the reigning Olympic champion. However, she will not have everything her own way. Werro has emerged as one of the biggest threats to Hodgkinson. The Swiss runner stunned Hodgkinson at the Stockholm Diamond League meeting in June. Werro won the race in 1:53.98, while Hodgkinson set a British record of 1:54.33. Werro then improved her personal best again in Paris three weeks later. She clocked 1:53.80 and strengthened her position as one of the leading 800m runners in the world. Hodgkinson, however, is not treating her Stockholm defeat as a setback. She believes the race showed how quickly the competition in the event is developing. The British star told Athletics Weekly that she is excited by the challenge and feels ready to compete. She admitted that June and July had been difficult at times, but added that she now feels in a strong place. Hodgkinson also pointed out that her Stockholm performance was still the fastest race of her career. She improved the British record by 0.28 seconds and believes that achievement should not be overlooked simply because she finished second. The 24-year-old also knows that championship racing can produce unexpected results. She recalled entering the Tokyo Olympics as the eighth-ranked athlete and leaving with a silver medal. On other occasions, she had started as the favourite but failed to win. That experience has taught Hodgkinson to approach major championships as a fresh challenge. She believes rankings and previous results do not always decide what happens on the track. title: 'Abusing is not cool': Manu Bhaker's social media post goes viral
text: Manu Bhaker (Image credit: Instagram) NEW DELHI: Double Olympic medallist Manu Bhaker has urged young people to avoid using abusive language, saying that "using bad language is not cool" and that the words people use reflect their personality. The 23-year-old shooter, who won two medals at the Paris Olympics, shared a long message on X on Sunday. She did not mention any particular incident but spoke about the increasing use of abusive language in everyday conversations. Watch Former BCCI CEO Rahul Johri on Indian cricket, IPL, media rights and more | Bombay Sport Exchange 'Choose your words wisely' Bhaker said people should be careful about the words they use because they shape a person's character over time. "The language we choose reflects our personality and the kind of person we are. Choose your words wisely, because over time, you become what you think, what you speak, and what you practice." "Using bad language is not cool. Abusing is not cool," she said. Bhaker also said that being "cool" has nothing to do with abusive language. "Let's keep the definition of cool simple: being hardworking, kind, respectful towards others and yourself, striving to be successful through honesty, and making your parents and your country proud. That's cool," the Indian shooter said. Bhaker later explained why she decided to speak about the issue. She said abusive language has slowly become normalised, especially among youngsters. "I'm speaking about this because, over the past few years, the way we perceive abusive language has changed. For many, using such words has become so normal that it's even considered 'cool'. Without realising it, people casually use degrading and disrespectful language in everyday conversations," Bhaker said.
